roots.name: Mainboard passive components
roots.description: The roughly 250-odd resistors, capacitors, trimmers and networks soldered to a Commodore 64 ASSY 250407 motherboard. No ICs, no connectors: only the two-terminal and adjustable parts that set the bias, timing and filtering of everything else on the board.
roots.note: Population figures are taken from a transcription of the 250407 bill of materials; Commodore shipped several board revisions (250407, 250425, 250466, 250469) and the exact mix of disc vs monolithic ceramic capacitors moved between them.

facts.label: Trimmers
facts.value: 1 x 500 ohm trimmer potentiometer (R27), 1 x variable capacitor

children.name: Resistors
children.description: Fixed resistors on the 250407: about seventy 1/4 W axial parts in values from 100 ohm to 1 megohm, plus four thick-film SIP resistor networks and one 500 ohm trimmer. Almost all were 5 percent carbon film; the handful of 1 percent metal film parts sat in the VIC-II colour and timing network.

facts.label: Package
facts.value: axial, 6.3 x 2.3 mm, 0.63 mm lead pitch

children.name: Discrete axial resistor families
children.description: Three manufacturing routes to a 1/4 W axial resistor coexisted in 1982. The 250407 used overwhelmingly carbon film; carbon composition was still common in cheaper consumer goods; metal film was reserved for precision.

children.name: Carbon film resistor (1/4 W axial)
children.description: The bulk of the board's resistors. A thin, discontinuous film of carbon and clay laid on a hollow alumina ceramic tube; carbon loading sets the resistance. Cheap, 5 percent, and tolerant of being bent during manual insertion.

facts.label: Resistance
facts.value: 1 ohm to 10 Mohm, here 100 ohm to 1 Mohm

children.name: Resistor slurry (carbon + clay + binder)
children.description: Carbon black mixed with china clay as a diluent and a phenolic binder in alcohol to a printable paste. Clay fraction is the coarse knob on resistance; binder keeps the film from flaking off the tube.
children.note: Clay here is kaolin, not the ball clay used in porcelain.

children.name: Carbon black (channel/process black)
children.description: Furnace black made by feeding heavy residual oil (or natural gas) into a hot air-cooled furnace so that it impinges and soots on water-cooled steel. Furnace black from petroleum feedstock was the standard conductive phase in resistors by the 1980s.

children.name: Carbon black furnace (soot reactor)
children.description: A refractory-lined combustion chamber with a ~1500 C flame and water-cooled steel scraper blades. Feed oil is sprayed across the flame; the resulting soot is scraped off as a mat and pelletised.

children.name: Petroleum residuum (heavy oil feed)
children.description: The heaviest fraction of an atmospheric or vacuum refinery distillation, a viscous bituminous residue rich in aromatics. Historically the feedstock for furnace black; later, natural gas.

children.name: Crude oil (refinery feed)
children.description: The whole hydrocarbon chain of the board terminates here: the carbon in the resistors, the epoxy and phenolic mouldings, the plastic film capacitors and the connector housings all began as crude.

children.name: Kaolin (china clay) diluent
children.description: Hydrated aluminium silicate, crushed and classified to a fine particle size. It is inert and non-conducting, so raising its share raises the sheet resistance of the dried film.

children.name: Kaolinite, Al2Si2O5(OH)4
children.description: The dioctahedral 1:1 clay mineral that gives kaolin its name. Formed by intense feldspar weathering and redeposition in kaolin pits.

children.name: Feldspar weathering front
children.description: Kaolin forms where granite and pegmatite decomposition leaves an acid-leached clay blanket. The parent rock is potassium-sodium aluminosilicate, typically mined as dimension stone or as a sand wash.

children.name: Phenolic binder resin in the slurry
children.description: Phenol-formaldehyde, dissolved in alcohol, holds carbon and clay to the tube and survives the 260 C cure. Cured phenolic also serves as the resistor's opaque body coating, which protects the film from humidity.
children.note: Some 1980s resistor makers switched the body coating to epoxy; the C64's were visually indistinguishable without a microscope.

children.name: Ceramic tube substrate
children.description: A thin-wall extruded alumina tube, 0.5 mm outside diameter, whose wall carries the film. Hollow construction halves the ceramic mass per resistor, and the tube's inner bore is what the trimmer's abrasive cut reaches.

children.name: Alumina (Al2O3) powder
children.description: 99 percent or better calcined alumina, the standard substrate for both resistor tubes and ceramic capacitor bodies. Strong, cheap, dimensionally stable, and electrically insulating.

children.name: Bauxite (aluminium ore)
children.description: The only ore that is predominantly aluminium. A soft, earthy, red-brown laterite of hydrated aluminium oxides (gibbsite, boehmite, diaspore) with iron and silica in the clay fraction. Roughly half of all aluminium ever smelted has come from bauxite.
children.note: The Weipa (Australia) and Boké (Guinea) deposits were the dominant bauxite sources in 1982.

facts.label: Al2O3 content
facts.value: 45-60 % typical, Guinea and Weipa ores the richest

facts.label: Formed by
facts.value: intense tropical chemical weathering of aluminous bedrock

children.name: Laterite and its parent rock
children.description: Bauxite is the end product of one of the most intense weathering processes on Earth: hot, wet, tropical conditions strip silica and alkalis out of clay and shale and leave the nearly insoluble aluminium hydroxides behind. The parent rock is often a clay or a weathered basalt, and the whole profile is metres thick.
children.note: Laterite hardens on exposure, which is why bauxite outcrops are quarried rather than dug, and why the term covers a family of tropical residual soils and ferricretes.

children.name: Bayer alumina refinery
children.description: Bauxite is crushed, digested in hot caustic soda to dissolve the alumina as sodium aluminate, the liquor is seeded with fine alumina to precipitate pure hydroxide, and the hydroxide is calcined at 1000-1300 C to finished 99.7 % alumina. Everything that does not dissolve - the red mud - is pumped to a tailings dam.

facts.label: Waste
facts.value: red mud, tens of tonnes per tonne of alumina

children.name: Caustic soda digestion
children.description: The Bayer process step that actually dissolves the ore: concentrated sodium hydroxide at pressure converts gibbsite to soluble sodium aluminate. NaOH was the dominant digestant because soda ash was cheaper; the potassium-hydroxide variant appeared in later residue-reduction schemes and is not the 1982 mainstream.

children.name: Tube extrusion and firing
children.description: Plasticised alumina is extruded through a die to a tube, cut to length on a flying saw, and fired in a tunnel kiln. Density is controlled so the film sees a reproducible surface.

children.name: Film deposition on the tube
children.description: The carbon-clay slurry is sprayed or dipped onto the rotating tube in a controlled spiral so the film lands only over the intended resistance length. Patterning the film length, not its thickness, is the primary way the value is dialled in.

children.name: Cure fire and carbonisation
children.description: A conveyor tunnel oven takes the coated tube to about 260 C, curing the phenolic and converting the carbonaceous binder to a stable conductive carbon film.

children.name: Axial lead termination (electroplate)
children.description: A lead is pushed down each end of the tube through the carbon film, and the assembly is barrel-plated in an electroless or electrolytic nickel bath so the film and lead make a low-resistance, solderable joint. In 1982 this was almost always nickel, sometimes with a thin silver flash.

children.name: Electroplating line (sulfamate / alkaline nickel)
children.description: Racks of resistors are plated in a barrel or belt line, then rinsed and dried. Plate thickness is the mechanical anchor that stops the lead being pulled out.

children.name: Electrolytic nickel plating bath
children.description: The lead and film are plated in a sulfamate or a Watts-type nickel bath. A sulfonamide-derived depolarising agent suppresses hydrogen evolution, so the deposit is ductile and the lead does not become brittle - which matters because a brittle lead snaps inside the resistor.

children.name: Nickel ore (laterite)
children.description: Garnierite, an hydrated nickel-magnesium silicate, is the classic ore. New Caledonia in the South Pacific and Cuba dominated world laterite supply in 1982, and the laterite is smelted to ferronickel rather than refined to pure nickel - the ferronickel then goes to a converter for the plating grade.
children.note: The nickel chain is carried in the metals file; this node exists so the plating bath has an origin.

children.name: Tinned copper lead wire
children.description: The axial lead is drawn copper wire, cut to length, tinned in a molten tin or tin-lead pot so the resistor dips cleanly in the wave-solder bath. Tinning is what stops the bare copper wire from oxidising between the barrel plating step and the board.

facts.label: Wire
facts.value: ~0.6 mm diameter, tinned in a 230-250 C pot

children.name: Value trimming (abrasive wheel)
children.description: A diamond wheel cuts a narrow slot through the film from the end of the tube, lengthening the resistive path a few micrometres at a time until the measured resistance hits the middle of the tolerance band. This is why carbon film resistors are called 'film' and why their tolerance is fixed after firing rather than before.

facts.label: Mechanism
facts.value: abrasive slot, NOT a laser scribing cut

children.note: Modern carbon film is still trimmed this way; laser trimming only ever made sense for thin film.

children.name: Abrasive cut-off wheel
children.description: A thin abrasive wheel, run at tens of thousands of revolutions per minute, cuts a slot through the film. Each pass lengthens the resistive path slightly; a few passes reach value.

children.name: Aluminium oxide abrasive
children.description: The standard grinding abrasive of the era, made by calcining alumina. Synthetic diamond was used only where the cut had to be finer.

children.name: Alumina from bauxite
children.description: Smelter-grade alumina, 99.5-99.7 % Al2O3, from the Bayer process. The substrate material for ceramic discs and MLCCs, the can material for resistors, and the dielectric feedstock for the barium titanate chain.

children.name: Bauxite profile
children.description: A soft, deeply weathered tropical profile of hydrated aluminium oxides; mined in open pits, often a few tens of metres thick, sitting directly on the aluminous bedrock.

children.name: Moulded epoxy body
children.description: The trimmed resistor is transfer-moulded in epoxy, or coated in a phenolic shell, sealing the film from humidity. Moulding compound is a phenolic or epoxy resin filled with silica flour.

children.name: Epoxy moulding of the resistor body
children.description: The resistor is placed in a transfer tool and encapsulated in epoxy resin cured at ~150-175 C for several minutes. Epoxy is chosen because it shrinks little and does not stress the film on cooling.

children.name: Offset-printed colour-code bands
children.description: The value and tolerance rings are printed on the epoxy body by an offset (rotogravure / dry-offset) coater using inks fired onto the surface. Three bands give significant figures, one multiplier, one tolerance. A 5 percent part gets a gold band; 1 percent gets brown.

facts.label: Colours
facts.value: black, brown, red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet, grey, white; gold, silver

facts.label: Method
facts.value: offset printing, ink cured onto epoxy

children.note: Bands are printed AFTER the part is trimmed and moulded - the trim determines the value, the print only reports it.

children.name: Band ink
children.description: Offset printing inks cured onto the epoxy body. The ink is a pigment in an oil and resin vehicle fired at a few hundred degrees so it will not rub off or solvent-attack during board cleaning.

children.name: Ink cure
children.description: The printed body is cured in a conveyor oven, not flame-fused. This is why the epoxy body has to be a thermoset: it has to survive the band-printing cure without flowing.

children.name: Carbon composition resistor
children.description: A rod of carbon and clay, compression-moulded into a small cylinder with metal end caps. Very cheap and very noisy, with a wide temperature coefficient and drift. Still used in 1982 in low-cost consumer goods and audio gear, but on the C64 itself it was already being displaced by carbon film.
children.note: Some very early Commodore boards (VIC-20, early PET) did use composition resistors; the 250407 does not appear to.

children.name: Composition mix (graphite + clay + binder)
children.description: A stiffer, higher-carbon paste than the film slurry. Because it is bulk rather than surface-conductive, the resistance is set by the geometry of the moulded rod itself, not by a pattern on its skin.

children.name: Diluent clay in the composition mix
children.description: A much higher clay fraction than in the film slurry, because a composition resistor has to be a weak conductor in bulk. Kaolin was the traditional diluent, the same mineral as in the film mix.

children.name: Kaolinite
children.description: Hydrated aluminium silicate, formed by intense feldspar weathering and worked from kaolin pits.

children.name: Feldspar weathering front
children.description: Kaolin forms where granite decomposition leaves an acid-leached clay blanket; the parent rock is mined as dimension stone or washed as sand.

children.name: Compression moulding
children.description: The mix is pressed in a matched-metal die at tens of tonnes to fill a slug shaped like a small pill, then baked. End caps of tin or brass are pressed on after cure.

children.name: Matched metal die
children.description: A matched-metal compression die with a cavity shaped like the finished slug. The cavity is chrome plated to survive the abrasive mix and the pressure.

children.name: Iron ore
children.description: Hematite and magnetite, the iron ore of the world trade. Everything ferrous in this file - springs, shafts, stamping dies, tool steel, cast-iron kiln parts - begins here.

children.name: Swaged metal end caps and wire leads
children.description: Soft tin or brass caps are pressed over the moulded slug, then a tinned copper wire lead is swaged inside the cap, giving the familiar bulbous ends of a composition resistor.
children.note: Lead wire is tin-plated copper drawn from rod, not tinned after the fact.

children.name: Tin for the end caps (cassiterite)
children.description: Tin is smelted from cassiterite, SnO2, the ore of tin. Because cassiterite is heavy and chemically inert it concentrates in placers and in alluvial tin streaming, and because cassiterite is dense it also accumulates in some alluvial gold deposits, where it was a nuisance.

children.name: Metal film resistor (1 % precision)
children.description: A NiCr or FeCr film vacuum-deposited onto an alumina substrate, then laser-trimmed to a tight tolerance. Where the VIC-II colour burst and the composite video level had to be set to a few parts in a thousand, a 1 percent metal film part was used instead of a 5 percent carbon film.
children.note: The 250407's parts list is dominated by 5 percent parts; I have not been able to confirm which individual reference designators were 1 percent metal film.

children.name: Flat ceramic substrate (not a tube)
children.description: Metal film parts use a flat alumina bar or a flat ceramic tube rather than a tube-with-a-skin, because the uniform flat substrate is what makes laser scribing produce a stable, precise spiral.

children.name: Metal-film substrate material
children.description: Metal film resistors need a very flat and very uniform substrate because the film resistance is set by the length of the deposited track, not by the substrate geometry. Alumina ceramic bar or a flat ceramic tube is used for that flatness.

children.name: Alumina from bauxite
children.description: Smelter-grade alumina, 99.5-99.7 % Al2O3, from the Bayer process. The substrate material for ceramic discs and MLCCs, the can material for resistors, and the dielectric feedstock for the barium titanate chain.

children.name: Bauxite profile
children.description: A soft, deeply weathered tropical profile of hydrated aluminium oxides; mined in open pits, often a few tens of metres thick, sitting directly on the aluminous bedrock.

children.name: NiCr resistance alloy
children.description: 80/20 nickel-chromium, or 75/25 iron-chromium, evaporated or sputtered from a heated wire or boat in a vacuum bell. NiCr is chosen for its bulk resistivity (~1.1 uohm-m) and, critically, for having a near-zero temperature coefficient of resistivity.
children.note: The chromium master alloy is itself a metallurgical product; I have not traced it to ore in this tree.

children.name: Chromium source (chromite)
children.description: The chromium in NiCr comes overwhelmingly from chromite, FeCr2O4, a hard black spinel mined from the Bushveld Complex and the Stillwater Complex in South Africa - then, as now, essentially the whole world supply. Ferrochrome is made in submerged-arc furnaces and shipped to the resistor alloy makers as 60-70 % Cr alloy.
children.note: South Africa supplied the majority of the world chrome ore consumed by the Western electronics industry in 1982.

children.name: Vacuum deposition bell
children.description: Parts are racked in a bell jar under vacuum; NiCr is evaporated at high current and condenses as a sub-micron film over the resistive area only, defined by an evaporated aluminium mask. Vacuum deposited - not sputtered - was standard for axial resistors in 1982.

children.name: Laser scribing of the spiral
children.description: A pulsed ruby or Nd:YAG laser ablates a thin groove across the film, lengthening the resistive path. A closed-loop measuring bridge runs thousands of cuts per second until the value converges. This - not a mechanical wheel - is what buys the 0.1-1 percent tolerance.

facts.label: Achievable tolerance
facts.value: 0.1-1 %, vs +/-5 % for a cut carbon film

children.name: Termination cap and lead
children.description: A crimped steel or aluminium cap grips the lead and makes contact with the film, then the whole assembly is plated in nickel. Metal film parts are always nickel-plated leads, never bare tin.

children.name: Termination cap material
children.description: A nickel-plated steel or aluminium cap, crimped onto the lead and forming the low-resistance joint to the film. Metal film parts are always nickel-plated leads: the plating has to be uniform for the part to be consistent.

children.name: Wirewound power resistor
children.description: Resistance wire wound on a ceramic bobbin and vitreously enamelled. Used for the few watts-and-above duties - notably the 7805 regulator's dropping resistor and the video level network. Accurate, stable, but large and inductive.
children.note: Wound resistors do not appear in the 250407 BOM I checked; included because they were the standard answer for the same problems in the C64's power supply and peripherals of the same era.

children.name: Ceramic bobbin
children.description: A grooved steatite or alumina former on which a length of enamelled resistance alloy wire is wound. Steatite (magnesium silicate) was the classic low-cost bobbin material.

children.name: Steatite bobbin material
children.description: Steatite, a compacted and fired magnesium silicate, was the classic low-cost bobbin and ceramic insulator material: it machines green, fires to a hard white body and is cheap.

children.name: Talc and soapstone
children.description: Steatite is a mixture of talc with clay. Talc is mined from metamorphosed dolomitic rock and is one of the few minerals still worked in a form close to its natural state.

children.name: Dolomitic host rock
children.description: Talc forms where magnesium-rich carbonate rock is metamorphosed; the talc is quarried from that host.

children.name: Vitreous enamel coating
children.description: The wound wire is coated in a glassy enamel and baked, which is why wirewounds are glassy-bodied. Continuous operation above about 200 C needs cement or silicone instead.

children.name: Vitreous enamel
children.description: A glassy coating on the wound wire, applied as a slurry and baked. The enamel is what makes a wirewound part look like a glass-bodied component and is what lets it run hot without the wire oxidising.

children.name: Silica sand
children.description: Quartz sand, the feedstock for glass, for frits and glazes, and for the hydrothermal growth of synthetic quartz. Dredged from beaches or quarried from ancient dune deposits.

children.name: Resistance alloy wire (NiCr / FeCr / CuNi)
children.description: Nichrome has the highest resistivity of the common resistance alloys and so minimises the wire length needed; constantan (CuNi) is used where a lower temperature coefficient matters more.
children.note: Constantan is 60/40 copper-nickel. Neither alloy is traced to ore here.

children.name: Metal-foil precision resistor
children.description: An ultra-precise resistor built from rolled, etched metal foil - nickel, a nickel-chromium-iron alloy, or copper - clamped between a rigid steel/ceramic case and a polished die. Changing the roll geometry stretches the foil, so the resistance can be set with a screw to one part in a million.
children.note: Included to explain the 'foil' end of the precision-resistor family. No metal-foil parts appear in a Commodore 64; these were calibration standards in the lab and appeared in later high-precision analogue equipment.

children.name: Etched metal foil roll
children.description: A strip of pure or alloy foil is rolled to a very tight radius on a mandrel and acid-etched to remove most of it, leaving fine islands of metal in series across the roll. The number of islands, not the sheet resistivity, sets the resistance.

children.name: Selective acid etch
children.description: The rolled foil is immersed in a ferric-nitrate or nitric-acid etch that removes most of it, leaving a fine grid of metal islands. Resistance is then set by the number of islands in the path, which is why foil resistors have their characteristic very high, very stable resistance values.

children.name: Nitric acid
children.description: A standard mineral acid made by the Ostwald process from ammonia oxidised over a platinum-rhodium gauze. Included here only to keep the chain honest.

children.name: Foil metal
children.description: Pure nickel or a nickel-iron-chromium alloy, chosen for a low temperature coefficient of resistivity and for its mechanical stability under tension.

children.name: Case, die and tension screw
children.description: The foil roll is sandwiched between a hardened case and a polished die with a slight bow. Turning the adjustment screw changes the roll's circumference, stretching the foil and raising the resistance by a controlled fraction of a part per million.
children.note: The polished die was lapped on cast iron with progressively finer abrasive; a diamond paste finish gives sub-micron flatness.

children.name: Lapped die surface
children.description: The die is lapped on cast iron with successively finer abrasive and finished with a sub-micron diamond polish. A die flat to a fraction of a micron is what lets the tension be controlled to a fraction of a part per million.

children.name: Thick-film cermet SIP resistor networks
children.description: The four resistor arrays on the 250407: two 8-way isolated 33 ohm packs (series terminators on the DRAM data bus), one 8-way 3k3 bussed pack and one 10-way 3k3 bussed pack. Each is one alumina substrate with several ruthenium-oxide resistive tracks screen-printed and fired together.
children.note: The parent brief mentioned a RIFA 481 resistor pack. RIFA (British Insulated Callender's Cables, Boxhill, UK) did supply SIP resistor networks to the European electronics trade in the 1980s, but I found no direct evidence that a RIFA 481 is fitted to a C64 mainboard - treat that specific part number as unverified. A Bourns 4308R-series or equivalent Vishay pack is the functionally correct part.

facts.label: Arrays on board
facts.value: 4 (RP1, RP2 = 33 ohm isolated 8-way; RP3 = 3k3 bussed 8-way; RP4 = 3k3 bussed 10-way)

children.name: Alumina substrate with printed elements
children.description: A 0.6 mm thick 96 percent alumina bar, pre-fired and metallised. Conductive paste is printed through a photo-plated stainless screen onto the top face only, then the whole bar is fired to fuse the glass frit and mature the resistor.

children.name: Thick-film conductor metallisation
children.description: A base-metal paste of finely divided silver or copper in a glass frit, screen-printed and fired at ~850 C to form the end lands, jumpers and common bus the resistive tracks connect to. Silver-palladium pastes were common in this era; copper pastes needed a nitrogen atmosphere to avoid oxidising.

facts.label: Base metal
facts.value: Ag or Ag-Pd (Ni-Pd-Ag common from the late 1980s)

children.note: Lead-free base metals such as Ni were not yet standard in 1982; the Ni-bearing pastes the prompt alludes to became common later.

children.name: Silver powder for the conductor paste
children.description: The conductor paste is fine silver flake or powder, not a bulk metal: it has to print as a paste and then fuse into a continuous conductor at 850 C without melting. Domestically mined silver was almost entirely gone by 1982; the metal was bought on the London spot market.

facts.label: Form
facts.value: atomised or electrolytic silver powder / flake, typically 99.9 %

children.name: Silver ore (argentite)
children.description: Silver came from argentite and other primary veins, but by 1982 a large and growing share of the world supply was a by-product of lead-zinc and copper refining - the metal recovered from anode slimes and residues rather than from its own mine. Mined silver is essentially a by-product metal.
children.note: The Mexico, Peru, US and Canadian mining districts were still significant, but lead-silver ore grades were so low by the 1980s that silver was economically a by-product of base-metal mining.

facts.label: Common ore
facts.value: argentite Ag2S; also pyrargyrite and stephanite

children.name: Tunnel-kiln firing of the printed bar
children.description: A continuous belt or pusher kiln takes the printed substrate through a controlled temperature ramp so the resistors are 'aged' in the firing. Thick-film resistors are typically driven 50 percent above their rating for 15-25 minutes to burn in the grain boundaries and stabilise the value.

children.name: Continuous kiln
children.description: A belt or pusher kiln with profiled hot zones, carrying the printed bar through drying, burnout, peak and controlled cooling. The cooling rate matters as much as the peak, because too fast a cool micro-cracks the glass.

children.name: Refractory kiln furniture
children.description: Alumina setters and shelves carrying the fired substrates through the kiln, themselves made from tabular alumina. Furnace furniture consumption is a real cost line in ceramics, and it comes from the same alumina as the substrate.

children.name: Alumina from bauxite
children.description: Smelter-grade alumina, 99.5-99.7 % Al2O3, from the Bayer process. The substrate material for ceramic discs and MLCCs, the can material for resistors, and the dielectric feedstock for the barium titanate chain.

children.name: Bauxite profile
children.description: A soft, deeply weathered tropical profile of hydrated aluminium oxides; mined in open pits, often a few tens of metres thick, sitting directly on the aluminous bedrock.

children.name: RuO2 cermet resistive paste
children.description: The resistive phase is sub-micron ruthenium dioxide powder blended with a lead-borosilicate glass frit and an organic vehicle (butyl acetate / terpineol) into a thixotropic paste. Its sheet resistance is a known function of powder loading, so a given RuO2 fraction sets a given ohms-per-square.
children.note: Ruthenium is a platinum-group metal, recovered as a by-product of platinum ores; it was the most expensive thing in a 1980s thick-film resistor and a genuine cost driver. The ore-to-powder chain is not traced here.

children.name: Ruthenium dioxide powder
children.description: Anhydrous RuO2 is the only resistor phase that survives to 900 C without oxidising away; the surrounding glass is what actually carries the current. Its scarcity set the price of every cermet resistor made in the 1980s.

children.name: Refining to capacitor-grade powder
children.description: The refinery dissolves platinum-group metal concentrate, precipitates the individual metals as ammonium or chloride salts, and reduces them to fine powder. Every step is a controlled chemical precipitation, and particle size is a sale specification in its own right.

children.name: Platinum-group ore bearing ruthenium
children.description: Ruthenium occurs almost only as a minor by-product in platinum and nickel ores (Merensky Reef, Sudbury, Norilsk) rather than in a ruthenium ore of its own. It reaches the resistor paste as ammonium ruthenium chloride after a complex refining sequence.
children.note: Coarse chain only; the ammonium ruthenium chloride route is my summary of standard refining practice, not a C64-specific fact.

children.name: Merensky Reef and nickel-copper sulphide ores
children.description: Ruthenium and the other platinum-group metals have no ore of their own. They occur at a few parts per million in the Merensky Reef of the Bushveld Complex and in the Sudbury and Norilsk nickel-copper sulphide ores, so the resistor industry bought ruthenium as a refinery by-product at platinum-group prices.

children.name: Chromitite layer
children.description: The Bushveld Reef sequence is layered, with a chromitite band, and ruthenium concentrates in that band. Its concentration is why South Africa, not Russia or Canada, supplied the ruthenium.

children.name: Screen printing through a photoemulsion
children.description: A stainless-steel mesh stretched over a frame, coated in photosensitive emulsion, contact-exposed through a film or direct-imaged artwork, developed, and then the paste squeegeed through the open areas onto the substrate. Line width is the resistance knob.

children.name: Stainless steel mesh
children.description: The printing screen is a woven stainless-steel or nylon mesh stretched over a frame and photo-imaged. Stainless was standard because it must survive repeated abrasion by the abrasive paste in the paste.

children.name: Iron ore
children.description: Hematite and magnetite, the iron ore of the world trade. Everything ferrous in this file - springs, shafts, stamping dies, tool steel, cast-iron kiln parts - begins here.

children.name: Paste rheology
children.description: A thixotropic paste is essential: it must flow under the squeegee and then stand without slumping, or the printed line will blur and the resistance will drift off value. Thixotropy comes from the shape of the glass frit particles.

children.name: Laser trimming of the network
children.description: An excimer or Nd:YAG laser ablates slots in each printed resistor until a closed-loop bridge calls out the right value. Bulk trimming can be 'slug' or 'v-cut' (pushing a wedge of resistive material aside) rather than ablating material away.
children.note: In 1982 a good fraction of commodity SIP networks were still trimmed by abrasive nozzle jet rather than laser.

children.name: Laser trimming system
children.description: A pulsed laser head over a moving substrate with an in-line ohmmeter, cutting and re-measuring thousands of times per second. Excimer lasers were used for fine-resolution cuts on thick films.

children.name: Laser source (Nd:YAG)
children.description: Neodymium:yttrium-aluminium-garnet was the standard solid-state laser for resistor trimming: a garnet crystal doped with neodymium, pumped optically and emitting at 1.06 microns. The yttrium-aluminium-garnet host is grown from alumina and yttrium oxide.

children.name: Alumina from bauxite
children.description: Smelter-grade alumina, 99.5-99.7 % Al2O3, from the Bayer process. The substrate material for ceramic discs and MLCCs, the can material for resistors, and the dielectric feedstock for the barium titanate chain.

children.name: Bauxite profile
children.description: A soft, deeply weathered tropical profile of hydrated aluminium oxides; mined in open pits, often a few tens of metres thick, sitting directly on the aluminous bedrock.

children.name: Epoxy potting and marking
children.description: The trimmed network is coated in a fire-resistant epoxy or phenolic varnish that also carries the colour code - here a small white dot or body colour denoting the resistance. Glass-filled epoxy was the standard SIP encapsulant.

children.name: Glass-filled epoxy coat
children.description: The whole array is coated in an epoxy loaded with fine glass or silica, which both seals the tracks and gives the package its mechanical rigidity. The colour body is the colourant in that coat.

children.name: Silica sand
children.description: Quartz sand, the feedstock for glass, for frits and glazes, and for the hydrothermal growth of synthetic quartz. Dredged from beaches or quarried from ancient dune deposits.

children.name: Lead frame
children.description: The array's leads are formed from a copper-alloy lead frame, plated in tin or solder, so the package can be inserted on a 2.54 mm pitch and wave-soldered.

children.name: Lead-frame plating
children.description: The copper-alloy leads are plated in tin or tin-lead so the array wavesolders cleanly. The frame is stamped from a coil in the same high-speed presses as the connector contacts.

children.name: Trim and adjustable resistors
children.description: The single adjustable part on the 250407 is R27, a 500 ohm cermet trimmer potentiometer that biases U31's crystal oscillator so the 14.31818 MHz colour subcarrier lands exactly on NTSC's subcarrier frequency. It is the reason a C64 needs no colour adjustment in normal use but will show colour shimmer when the crystal ages.
children.note: On later C64 boards (the '8710' revision and Commodore's own C64C), this variable resistor was replaced with a trimmer capacitor in the crystal's load network. Both do the same job: pulling the oscillator to exactly the right frequency.

facts.label: Tolerance
facts.value: +/-10 % body; the ADJUSTMENT is what matters

children.name: Cermet resistive element and track
children.description: A thick-film RuO2 resistive track deposited on the top face of an alumina substrate, with a metal-foil wiper that slides along it. Because the element is a printed film rather than a carbon blob, the tracking is smooth and the part does not develop a scratchy potentiometer feel the way a carbon composition pot does.

facts.label: Wiper
facts.value: Ni alloy or precious metal, fork or blade

children.name: Wiper alloy
children.description: A nickel-alloy or precious-metal spring contact rubbing on the RuO2 film. Because the cermet element is hard, the wiper is deliberately the sacrificial element and is made of a soft, wear-resistant alloy.

children.name: Nickel ore
children.description: Laterite ore, the origin of the wiper alloy as well as the plating and the MLCC internal electrode.

children.name: Electrical travel and resolution
children.description: The usable travel is a fraction of the physical length because the track is designed to have most of its resistance in the middle of the sweep. That is how a 500 ohm trimmer gets a usable 0-500 ohm range from a single turn of an adjuster screw.

children.name: Adjuster screw and slider
children.description: A knurled brass or stainless screw drives a moulded slider that rides the wiper along the track. Backing-off epoxy locks the setting once the board is aligned.

children.name: Adjuster screw
children.description: A brass or stainless screw, knurled or slotted, driving the slider. Brass is the usual choice because it machines cleanly at small diameters and does not gall against the moulded slider.

children.name: Copper ore to brass
children.description: Cartridge brass from copper and zinc ore; the same alloy as the connector contact strip.

children.name: Epoxy lock
children.description: After alignment a drop of epoxy is flowed over the adjuster so the setting cannot drift in service. On a machine with no calibration facility this trimmer is effectively a one-time factory adjustment for forty years.

children.name: Locking epoxy
children.description: A drop of epoxy flowed over the adjuster and allowed to cure hard. It is a destructive, deliberate lock: once the trim is set on the factory line, that trimmer is not adjustable again.

children.name: Capacitors
children.description: The mainboard's decoupling, timing, filtering and coupling capacitors. Overwhelmingly ceramic (0.1 uF bypass plus small timing values), with a smaller tail of aluminium electrolytics for the low-frequency supplies and film polyester for the SID output coupling.

facts.label: Ceramic
facts.value: ~54 x 0.1 uF/50 V plus 15-1800 pF timing caps

facts.label: Electrolytic
facts.value: ~15 x 10 uF/25 V radial + larger 100-2200 uF axial

children.name: Monolithic ceramic capacitor (MLCC)
children.description: The 0.1 uF bypass and small timing capacitors. Dozens of layers of barium-titanate ceramic with screen-printed metal electrodes buried between them, then fired and terminated. Monolithic construction gives huge capacitance in a tiny body because the electrode area is the whole face of every layer.
children.note: The 250407 parts list as transcribed by the replica-board project specifies 0.1 uF 50 V X7R, 0.22 uF Z5U and small C0G parts; Commodore's exact mix of ceramic disc versus monolithic changed between board revisions, and the X7R/Z5U designations are modern restatements of what were then simply 'ceramic'.

facts.label: Dielectric classes
facts.value: X7R / Z5U for the big values, C0G for the small timing caps

facts.label: Size (1982)
facts.value: ~2.5 x 3.2 mm radial blocks and discs

children.name: Barium titanate dielectric powder
children.description: The heart of the MLCC: sub-micron BaTiO3 crystallites, the only powder that has a very high dielectric constant AND survives the high-temperature processing. Chemistry is shifted from pure BaTiO3 by dopants to move the Curie point below room temperature, giving a Class II (X7R/Z5U) part with high capacitance that still decays with temperature.

facts.label: Particle size
facts.value: ~0.2-1 um; coarse-grain BaTiO3 was typical of early-1980s X7R

children.note: Y5V, also a Class II code, is real but was not the dominant 1982 designation; the breadbin C64 parts are best described as X7R/Z5U-era ceramics.

children.name: Solid-state BaTiO3 synthesis
children.description: Barium carbonate and titanium dioxide are ball-milled with the dopants in water to a homogeneous slurry, then calcined in a kiln at about 1050-1200 C. The carbonate decomposes and the perovskite BaTiO3 crystallises. The mass is reground and wet-milled with a dispersant down to the target particle size.
children.note: The brief's '1150-1250 C' is the right order of magnitude for the calcination fire; I have narrowed it slightly.

children.name: Barium carbonate (BaCO3) feed
children.description: Made by carbonating barium sulfide solution, or by precipitation from soluble barium salts. Barite is the natural source: it is beneficiated, reduced to BaS and carbonated back to the carbonate.

children.name: Barite (BaSO4), mined
children.description: Heavy-spar ore, usually a vein or cavity filler in limestone and evaporite, mined underground. It is the world source of essentially all barium and therefore of the barium in every BaTiO3 MLCC.
children.note: Morocco, China, Mexico and India were the leading barite producers of the early 1980s.

children.name: Titanium dioxide (TiO2) feed
children.description: Ceramic-grade TiO2, made by chlorinating ilmenite or rutile to TiCl4 and re-oxidising, or by sulphuric acid digestion. Low-iron pigment-grade material is used so the fired ceramic has good insulation resistance.

children.name: Ilmenite (FeTiO3) sand
children.description: A black, heavy placer sand mined from beach and dune deposits. The principal titanium ore, either smelted to high-titanium slag or chlorinated directly to pigment.
children.note: Australia was the dominant ilmenite supplier to the ceramic-grade pigment chain in 1982.

children.name: Donor / acceptor doping
children.description: Trivalent donor dopants (La2O3, Dy2O3, Y2O3) or pentavalent acceptors (Nb2O5, Ta2O5, Sb2O5) are added during calcination. Donors leave the ceramic 'depleted' so the grains sit uniformly in the paraelectric phase at room temperature, which gives the stable, moderate-loss X7R curve. Acceptor dopants raise the Curie point so the material stays ferroelectric and gives a much higher, more temperature-sensitive Z5U.
children.note: The physics is standard ceramics; the specific dopant-to-Class assignments are my summary and are flagged medium.

children.name: Rare-earth dopant oxides
children.description: Lanthanum, dysprosium and yttrium oxides, ground and sieved to sub-micron, are the donor dopants that set the temperature coefficient of an X7R dielectric. They are rare-earth minerals mined and separated in small tonnages, and their price was a visible line item in MLCC costing.

children.name: Bastnaesite (monazite and bastnaesite concentrates)
children.description: Rare-earth minerals are worked chiefly from carbonatite and monazite/bastnaesite concentrates, with the world supply dominated by one mining complex and its associated separation plants. The oxides are then produced by acid leach and solvent extraction.
children.note: The rare-earth separation chain is complex; flagged medium because I have deliberately compressed it.

children.name: Tape-casting slurry (powder + frit + binder)
children.description: The BaTiO3 powder is blended with a glass frit - an aid to sintering and to dielectric strength at the electrode interface - and an organic binder into a homogeneous, flowable slip. In 1982 this was an acrylic or PVA binder in water, or a cellulose ester in an organic solvent; fully water-based PVA systems became dominant later.

facts.label: Glass frit
facts.value: ~5 % by weight of the ceramic body

children.name: Glass frit in the slurry
children.description: A few per cent of low-melting glass, added so that on sintering it wets the barium titanate grains, closes the porosity and gives the internal electrode a hermetic interface. Without it the MLCC is not gas-tight and its insulation resistance collapses.

children.name: Silica sand
children.description: Quartz sand, the feedstock for glass, for frits and glazes, and for the hydrothermal growth of synthetic quartz. Dredged from beaches or quarried from ancient dune deposits.

children.name: Tape casting to green sheets
children.description: The slip is doctor-bladed onto a moving polyester carrier film to a controlled dry thickness. This single step sets the eventual capacitance density, because capacitance is dielectric thickness divided by the number of electrode layers stacked.

facts.label: Green sheet thickness
facts.value: ~1-10 um; early-1980s parts often cast 5-20 um

children.note: Correcting the brief slightly: the 1-10 um figure is modern; 1982 parts cast thicker, coarser sheets to keep the layer count and the cost of handling down.

children.name: Moving carrier belt
children.description: The green sheet is carried on a continuous polyester belt and dried in a short oven as the doctor blade lays it down, so the green thickness is set by blade clearance against a moving web rather than by a single-shot cast.

children.name: Doctor blade
children.description: A precisely-ground steel or ceramic blade with a controlled edge angle, set to micrometres over the belt. The single most important tool in MLCC making: it sets layer thickness and therefore capacitance density.

children.name: Screen-printing internal electrodes
children.description: A metal paste is printed onto the green sheets to define the buried internal electrodes. In 1982 the commodity MLCC used a base-metal nickel paste fired in a low-pO2 atmosphere, because silver would diffuse down the grain boundaries of the BaTiO3 and wreck its insulation resistance. The older, more expensive palladium-silver internal electrodes the brief mentions were by 1982 largely a legacy technology kept for a few high-reliability parts.

facts.label: Legacy alternative
facts.value: PdAg, mostly phased out by the early 1980s

facts.label: Print
facts.value: screen through a photoemulsion mask, offset on high-volume lines

children.note: This is the one place where the brief's chemistry needed correcting: PdAg was the 1960s-70s internal electrode, not the 1980s one. Nickel-Pd-Ag composite pastes (Ni with a Pd-Ag core) only became the standard after about 1985.

children.name: Base-metal nickel paste
children.description: The internal electrode paste: finely divided nickel in a glass frit and an organic vehicle, screen-printed onto the green sheet and co-fired with the ceramic. Nickel was chosen over silver for cost and over palladium for cost, and it is what let a 0.1 uF 50 V bypass capacitor be sold for a fraction of a cent.

children.name: Nickel from its ore, in the plating and paste supply chain
children.description: The nickel in a nickel internal electrode came ultimately from laterite ore or from nickel matte imported as an intermediate. By 1982 the intermediate trade in ferronickel and matte was a well-developed global market, which is why a capacitor cost in Hong Kong was sensitive to South African chrome and New Caledonian nickel.
children.note: This is an economic description of the supply chain rather than a specific process step; flagged medium deliberately.

children.name: Stacking, lamination and debinding
children.description: The printed green sheets are stacked offset so every sheet's electrode lands alternately on the two opposed faces, then compressed in a hydraulic laminator and the organic binder burned out slowly. The result is a monolithic bar of hundreds of ceramic layers with the electrodes sealed inside.

facts.label: Layers
facts.value: ~10-60 active layers for a 1982 0.1 uF 50 V part

facts.label: Debinding
facts.value: slow ramp 200-400 C to avoid cracking the stack

children.name: Hydraulic laminator
children.description: A heated hydraulic press that stacks and consolidates hundreds of sheets at once, aligned by registration pins. This is the step that turns a pile of loose printed film into one solid bar.

children.name: Layer registration
children.description: Each successive sheet is offset by exactly the margin width so that the printed electrodes line up alternately with the two opposed faces. Nothing in a modern capacitor is more precise than this stack-up.

children.name: Dicing into blanks
children.description: The laminated bar is cut with a resin-bonded diamond saw into hundreds or thousands of identical blanks, each one capacitor body. This is why MLCC manufacture is a barrel process: one sintered bar yields thousands of capacitors, and the economics only work at that scale.

children.name: Resin-bonded diamond blade
children.description: A thin, flat, run-of-the-mill diamond wheel; the same abrasive technology as the crystal grinder but applied to a sintered ceramic bar.

children.name: Synthetic diamond abrasive
children.description: Industrial diamond in 1982 was made almost entirely by shock-wave synthesis from graphite, and its price set the cost of grinding, drilling and sawing across the whole ceramics and glass industry.

children.name: Barrel economics
children.description: One sintered bar yields thousands of capacitors and one furnace run yields many bars. The economics only work at that scale, which is why MLCC production consolidated into a handful of very large Japanese, European and later Taiwanese plants by the early 1980s.

children.name: Firing in a continuous belt kiln
children.description: The blanks go through a continuous belt or pusher kiln under a controlled low oxygen partial pressure, so the ceramic sinters dense and hermetic while the nickel internal electrodes are not oxidised away. Density matters enormously: a porous body lets moisture attack the electrode stack and destroys the insulation resistance.

facts.label: Atmosphere
facts.value: low pO2 / forming gas or N2

children.note: Two kiln temperatures in the brief refer to two different operations: 1150-1250 C is the BaTiO3 powder calcination, ~1300 C is the finished body's sinter. Both are right for their step.

children.name: Kiln heating elements
children.description: Silicon-carbide or nichrome elements in a continuous belt kiln held at ~1300 C for hours. Long soaks at high temperature are what drive the ceramic to theoretical density.

children.name: Low-oxygen atmosphere
children.description: A forming-gas or nitrogen atmosphere with a controlled oxygen partial pressure, just low enough that nickel does not oxidise but high enough that the organic binder burns off cleanly. Getting this window right is the hardest part of base-metal MLCC manufacture.

children.name: End terminations (nickel + solderable outer)
children.description: After firing, the two exposed end faces are terminated with a conducting band that collects current from the hundreds of buried electrodes. In 1982 this was a fired-on or sputtered nickel layer with a solderable silver or tin outer layer, or a simple dipped solder band. The C64 boards were wave-soldered in tin-lead, so the termination had to wet 63/37 solder.

facts.label: 1982 termination
facts.value: Ni barrier with Ag or Ni-Sn outer layer, or dipped tin-lead solder

facts.label: Modern difference
facts.value: pure sintered Ni-Sn terminations with no precious metal are today's standard

children.note: I am confident about the nickel barrier plus solderable outer layer; I am less sure which of the outer-layer options Commodore's capacitor supplier used in 1982.

children.name: Tin for the solderable termination
children.description: The outer termination layer has to wet 63/37 lead-tin solder in a wave bath, so it is tin or tin-silver. Tin came from cassiterite, and the whole world electronics industry in 1982 was competing for the same tin that solder and bronze also needed.
children.note: The cassiterite chain is at mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.carbon-composition.end-cap.tin; referenced rather than duplicated.

children.name: Aluminium electrolytic capacitor
children.description: The polarised bulk capacitors: about fifteen 10 uF/25 V radial parts decoupling the SID and video analogue rails, plus larger axial 100-2200 uF parts on the rectified supply rails. Value comes from a nanometres-thick anodic oxide on etched aluminium foil soaked in electrolyte - cheap, large capacitance, and the bulk of the board's supply-rail filtering.

facts.label: Radial parts
facts.value: ~15 x 10 uF/25 V, 5 x 5 mm can

children.name: High-purity anode foil, rolled and etched
children.description: 99.5 %+ aluminium foil, chemically etched in a hot hydrochloric/nitric acid or chlorate bath to grow microscopic pits on the surface. Effective cathode area rises by a factor of fifty to a hundred, which is how a hundred microfarads fits into a 5 mm can.

facts.label: Etchant
facts.value: hot HCl/HNO3, or a sodium chlorate bath

children.name: Anodic formation (the real dielectric)
children.description: The etched foil is made the anode in a phosphoric or boric acid bath at 90-200 V DC, growing a barrier-type aluminium oxide layer tens of nanometres thick. The rated working voltage of the finished capacitor is just the voltage the oxide can hold, so higher ratings need a thicker oxide and hence less capacitance for the same area.

facts.label: Forming voltage
facts.value: ~90-200 V DC for parts rated 6-50 V

children.name: Phosphoric acid from phosphate rock
children.description: The phosphate acid in the forming bath fixes the oxide growth characteristics. It is made by burning rock phosphate - calcium phosphate from sedimentary apatite deposits - in a furnace and absorbing the fumes in water.

children.name: Anode foil from re-melted foil-mill scrap
children.description: Rolled foil offcuts, edge trim and rejected capacitor-grade foil were re-smelted in a holding furnace and re-rolled into fresh anode foil rather than being returned to the general scrap stream. That closed loop is why capacitor makers were, in effect, recycling their own aluminium, and why an aluminium price move showed up in 1982 capacitor prices with a lag.
children.note: Closed-loop recycling of capacitor foil scrap was standard practice, but prime foil from the primary smelter was still used for the tightest-tolerance parts; I cannot say which proportion applied to Commodore's 1982 supply.

children.name: Primary aluminium from bauxite
children.description: The other half of the loop: alumina from bauxite, smelted in a Hall-Héroult cell by dissolving it in molten cryolite and electrolytising at ~950-970 C. The cathode metal is 99.7 % pure and it is this, or re-melted scrap of it, that rolls into capacitor anode foil.

children.name: Cryolite (Na3AlF6) from fluorspar
children.description: The bath solvent that lets aluminium be smelted below its own melting point. Cryolite is made synthetically from hydrofluoric acid and alumina, and the hydrofluoric acid historically came from fluorspar - a calcium fluoride mineral mined in Mexico, South Africa and China.

children.name: Cathode foil
children.description: Aluminium foil, usually a cheaper alloy and often unetched, serving as the return electrode. It carries no dielectric of its own; its job is simply to collect the return current through the electrolyte.

children.name: Cathode foil rolling
children.description: High-purity aluminium rolled to a few tens of microns, often lightly etched, slit into ribbons for the winding. It uses the same aluminium as the anode but a looser specification, because no dielectric quality depends on it.

children.name: Alumina from bauxite
children.description: Smelter-grade alumina, 99.5-99.7 % Al2O3, from the Bayer process. The substrate material for ceramic discs and MLCCs, the can material for resistors, and the dielectric feedstock for the barium titanate chain.

children.name: Bauxite profile
children.description: A soft, deeply weathered tropical profile of hydrated aluminium oxides; mined in open pits, often a few tens of metres thick, sitting directly on the aluminous bedrock.

children.name: Working electrolyte
children.description: The conducting liquid that soaks the separator and carries current between the oxide and the cathode: boric or phosphoric acid dissolved in ethylene glycol, dimethylformamide or dimethyl sulfoxide. The solvent must wet the porous separator without dissolving or attacking the oxide, and the acid concentration sets the oxide's equilibrium thickness.

children.name: Boric acid in the electrolyte
children.description: Boric acid sets the oxide chemistry of the anode and, with phosphoric acid, is the reason an aluminium electrolytic has a usable voltage range at all. Commercially it was made from borax, which is mined from evaporite deposits.

facts.label: Key deposits
facts.value: California (US), Turkey, Chile - the US borates led world supply in 1982

children.name: Borax (tincalconite) evaporite
children.description: Sodium tetraborate decahydrate occurs in the playas and evaporite deposits of closed desert basins, where boron-bearing volcanic hot springs have fed an evaporating lake for millions of years. It is mined, not synthesised, in the borate districts.

children.name: Glycol-ether solvent from petrochemistry
children.description: Ethylene glycol and the glycol ethers used as high-voltage capacitor solvents were derived from ethylene oxide, itself made by oxidising ethylene from a steam cracker. They replaced the glycol-ester electrolytes of the 1950s because they dissolve the anode oxide without attacking it.
children.note: The refining chain itself is expanded in the plastics and chemicals files.

facts.label: Route
facts.value: crude -> steam cracking -> ethylene -> ethylene oxide -> glycol ether

children.name: Ethylene glycol ethers from ethylene oxide
children.description: Ethylene oxide is made by direct oxidation of ethylene over a silver or chromite catalyst, then reacts with an alcohol to give the glycol ether. The solvent chemistry of an aluminium electrolytic is therefore set two or three steps downstream of a steam cracker.

children.name: Naphtha
children.description: The light distillate between gasoline and kerosene, and the standard cracker feed. A refinery fraction of crude, not a geological product.

children.name: Separator (paper or polyolefin)
children.description: A porous, electrolyte-wicking separator keeping the foils apart while letting current through. Bleached kraft paper was still the standard for most 1980s aluminium electrolytics; low-porosity oriented polypropylene or polyethylene sleeves were the premium, longer-life alternative.

facts.label: 1982 default
facts.value: bleached kraft paper; PE/PP sleeves for higher-reliability parts

facts.label: Why it matters
facts.value: the separator is the main leakage path and electrolyte reservoir

children.note: Correcting the brief: paper was still the volume material in 1982. Polypropylene separators had been commercial for years but were not yet dominant.

children.name: Bleached kraft paper separator
children.description: A very thin, very porous cellulose tissue wound between the foils. It must be wetted completely by the electrolyte but must not contain ions that would raise the leakage current, so it is washed and bleached before use. Kraft paper separators are why the electrolyte is held in place at all.

facts.label: Why paper
facts.value: absorbent, cheap, dimensionally stable when wetted

children.name: Wood pulp
children.description: Kraft paper is made from softwood (long-fibre) pulped in the kraft process. Because the separator is a fraction of a gram of tissue it uses a negligible mass of wood, but it is one of the very few places where a C64 is literally made of a tree.

children.name: Winding on a mandrel and impregnation
children.description: Anode foil, separator and cathode foil are wound together on a rotating mandrel into a compact roll. Electrolyte is then vacuum- or pressure-impregnated into the wound roll, filling every pore and pushing out air, which is what finally gives the part its capacitance.

facts.label: Impregnation
facts.value: vacuum impregnation, repeated 2-4 times to drive out trapped air

facts.label: Slitting
facts.value: cathode foil is slit into two or three ribbons for a multi-section winding

children.name: Winding mandrel
children.description: A polished steel mandrel, often Teflon-coated, on which the foil sandwich is wound. Mandrel diameter and surface finish are set by the smallest foil thickness so the finished pack can be released without creasing.

children.name: Iron ore
children.description: Hematite and magnetite, the iron ore of the world trade. Everything ferrous in this file - springs, shafts, stamping dies, tool steel, cast-iron kiln parts - begins here.

children.name: Winding pitch and section count
children.description: The number of anode/cathode sections and their winding pitch set the ripple current behaviour and the ESR of the finished part, which is why a low-ESR part is physically bigger than a same-value general-grade one.

children.name: Crimping, sleeving and end-fill bung
children.description: Aluminium or tinned-copper alloy terminal tabs are crimped onto the anode and cathode edges of the wound pack. The pack is then sleeved - PVC heat-shrink or a printed cardboard outer - and sealed at the end with a rubber or PVC bung that retains the electrolyte against its expansion over temperature. The paper and foil layers you see when you cut one open are the winding itself.

facts.label: Terminal
facts.value: crimped Al or Cu alloy tab; anode polarity marked on the sleeve

facts.label: Sleeve
facts.value: PVC heat-shrink or printed cardboard outer

children.name: End-fill bung
children.description: A rubber or PVC disc that fills the end of the sleeve and retains the electrolyte against thermal expansion and the internal pressure generated during burn-in. It is the visible rubber disc at the base of a radial electrolytic.

children.name: Silicone rubber bung
children.description: Heat-cured silicone rubber, chosen because it stays soft and chemically inert in contact with the acid electrolyte for decades. Silicone is a siloxane polymer built on a quartz-derived silicon-oxygen backbone.

children.name: Silica sand
children.description: Quartz sand, the feedstock for glass, for frits and glazes, and for the hydrothermal growth of synthetic quartz. Dredged from beaches or quarried from ancient dune deposits.

children.name: Aluminium terminal tab
children.description: A soft aluminium or aluminium-alloy tab, crimped onto the foil edge. Pure aluminium is used because it is the only metal that will not form a galvanic or resistive joint with the foil it must touch.

children.name: Aluminium purity of the tab
children.description: Capacitor tabs and foils are made from very high-purity aluminium; iron and silicon above a few tenths of a per cent make the alloy hard and prone to sludge in the electrolyte, so capacitor-grade purity is stricter than structural grade.

children.name: Ageing and burn-in
children.description: Finished parts are held at an elevated temperature under DC bias so the oxide re-thickens and the leakage current settles. A 1980s capacitor arrives already partly formed, which is why an electrolytic recovered from a two-year-old Commodore machine often measures better than a brand-new one straight from a 2020s reel.

facts.label: Burn-in
facts.value: ~1-2x rated voltage at 85-125 C, hours to days

facts.label: Effect
facts.value: reduces initial leakage and stabilises capacitance

children.name: Burn-in chamber
children.description: A temperature-controlled rack of trays in which finished parts are held at temperature and bias. A good capacitor plant in 1982 might burn in for hours or days, which is why vintage electrolytics so often arrive already formed.

children.name: Capacitance and leakage test
children.description: Parts are tested for capacitance, dissipation factor and leakage at rated temperature. Rejection rates in a commodity 10 uF 25 V part were small but non-zero, and every rejected part was a loss of scrap aluminium.

children.name: Capacitance and dissipation-factor measurement
children.description: A bridge or LCR meter at rated frequency and temperature gives capacitance and dissipation factor; a DC bias step gives leakage. Rejection on leakage is what catches a pinhole in the oxide, the classic failure mode of a fresh electrolytic.

children.name: Tantalum capacitor
children.description: A polarised capacitor built around sintered tantalum powder with an anodic oxide dielectric and a solid electrolyte. Low leakage and very good stability for its size; in the early 1980s tantalum was the default decoupling choice on high-performance professional digital boards.
children.note: The breadbin C64 250407 uses aluminium electrolytics and ceramics, NOT tantalum on its logic. Tantalum was standard in the same period's professional and instrumentation designs and appears elsewhere in Commodore hardware of the era. Included for era breadth and for the tantalum supply story; do not read it as mainboard content.

children.name: Sintered tantalum anode
children.description: Capacitor-grade tantalum powder is pressed around a tantalum wire anode lead and sintered at 1200-1400 C under vacuum, producing a porous body with an enormous internal surface area. The Ta2O5 dielectric then grows on that surface, which is why a gram of powder stores far more capacitance than a gram of film.

children.name: Drawn tantalum wire
children.description: The anode lead is fine drawn tantalum wire, spot-welded to the sintered pellet. Tantalum wire was drawn by the same machinery as refractory metals for furnace leads, from the same powder-to-wire routes.

children.name: Capacitor-grade tantalum metal and oxide
children.description: Whether the anode is built from reduced metallic powder or from sintered oxide powder, the specification is the same: extremely high purity, sub-micron, high surface area. Impurities here are the defect mechanism that causes tantalum dielectric failures.

children.name: Columbite-tantalite concentrate
children.description: The concentrate that becomes capacitor-grade powder. Every stage from ore to powder discards most of the feed, which is why tantalum capacitors had a high metal cost per cubic centimetre even in 1982.

children.name: Anode pressing and sintering
children.description: Powder is blended with a binder and pressed around the wire, then debound and sintered in vacuum or flowing hydrogen at 1200-1400 C. The pressed pellet is deliberately porous - roughly half its volume is void - because that void is where the dielectric forms.

children.name: Anodic Ta2O5 formation and MnO2 solid electrolyte
children.description: The sintered anode is anodised to grow the Ta2O5 dielectric, then coated with manganese dioxide by pyrolytically decomposing manganese chloride vapour on the surface - the classic 1980s solid tantalum part. A sintered silver-paste counter-electrode existed as an alternative construction. Today's conductive-polymer tantalum is a late-1990s development.

facts.label: Counter-electrode
facts.value: MnO2 from MnCl2 pyrolysis (standard); sintered Ag paste (alternative)

facts.label: Forming
facts.value: ~50-200 V DC sets the working voltage

children.note: The brief lists silver paste as the solid counter-electrode; the standard 1980s solid tantalum counter-electrode was MnO2. Both constructions existed, so this is a correction of emphasis rather than of substance.

children.name: Manganese chloride for pyrolysis
children.description: MnCl2 is vapour-decomposed on the hot tantalum surface in a furnace at several hundred degrees, leaving a conformal MnO2 layer that acts as the solid counter-electrode. The chloride is shipped as a hydrate and is hygroscopic, so it had to be kept dry.

children.name: Manganese ore (pyrolusite)
children.description: Manganese came from pyrolusite and other oxide ores, and mostly as a by-product of the iron and steel industry, since most manganese ore is mined to be alloyed into steel rather than for its own sake.

children.name: Forming voltage and working rating
children.description: The anode is anodised at a voltage above its rated working voltage, usually by a factor of 1.5-2, to build a defect-free oxide. The rated voltage of the part is set by that formation step and is not adjustable afterwards.

children.name: The counter-electrode body
children.description: Below the manganese dioxide sits the original tantalum anode body and its second termination. The layer stack is metal, dielectric, counter-electrode, then a conductive path to the case - all inside an epoxy dip.

children.name: Tantalum lead, braze and epoxy seal
children.description: The anode lead is drawn tantalum wire, spot-welded to the sintered pellet, then the assembly is sealed by an epoxy dip. On wet-slug types the hermetic case is glass or a welded metal can with a Teflon ring seal. The part is then marked with its value, rating and the manufacturer.

facts.label: Anode lead
facts.value: drawn tantalum wire, spot-welded to the pellet

facts.label: Braze
facts.value: silver or silver-graphite drop for the lead joint; Ta-Au braze on some types

facts.label: Seal
facts.value: epoxy dip for solid types; welded metal can for wet-slug types

children.name: Epoxy dip seal
children.description: Solid tantalum parts were sealed by dipping in epoxy and curing, which protects the brittle MnO2/dielectric stack against handling and moisture. Wet-slug parts instead used a welded metal can with a glass or Teflon seal.

children.name: Epoxy resin and bisphenol A
children.description: The standard epoxy of the period: bisphenol A condensed with epichlorohydrin, cured with an amine. Both halves are petrochemical, and bisphenol A was the dominant resin for adhesive, coating, printed-board and capacitor sealants alike.

children.name: Benzene from a steam cracker
children.description: Aromatic hydrocarbon recovered from the aromatics complex of a large cracker or from catalytic reforming of naphtha. The root of styrene, phenol, cumene, aniline and bisphenol.

children.name: Value and rating marking
children.description: The dipped part was marked along its length with the capacitance, rated voltage, tolerance, manufacturer and date code, usually by ink printing on the epoxy.

children.name: Early-1980s tantalum supply squeeze
children.description: Capacitor tantalum depends on columbite-tantalite ore, essentially all of it from the Kivu region of Zaire and neighbouring Rwanda and Burundi. A collapse in the electronics market in 1982-83 drained the supply chain's stocks, then demand spiked again in 1984 on the PC and automotive booms. The USGS records a significant spike in tantalum demand in 1984, with US factory sales of tantalum capacitors at an all-time high and escalating prices pushing consumers to substitute aluminium parts and to design tantalum out where they could. It was a real, documented shortage in exactly the C64's production window.
children.note: The 1984 demand spike and the all-time-high factory sales figure are verified against USGS Circular OF01-349. I have deliberately not stated a peak capacitor-grade powder price for 1983-84 because I could not source a reliable figure for that specific grade and year.

children.name: Capacitor-grade recycling loop
children.description: Because tantalum metal is expensive, tantalum-bearing scrap - rejected capacitors, anode dust, trimmed pellet scrap - was recovered and returned to the powder supply. This is why a 1983-84 shortage hit prices so hard: recycled powder could not be substituted for virgin powder in a dielectric that had to be defect-free.

children.name: Engineering response to the squeeze
children.description: The documented response was to reduce tantalum content where possible, substitute aluminium electrolytics, and lengthen qualified lead times. It is a good example of how a metals shortage propagates into board design decisions within eighteen months.

children.name: Columbite ore to capacitor-grade powder
children.description: Columbite-tantalite ore is digested in hydrofluoric acid in an autoclave at 100-200 C to dissolve the tantalum as a fluorotantalate, the solution is treated with potassium chloride or potassium hydroxide to precipitate K2Ta2O7, and that intermediate is converted to a metallic or oxide powder by sodium reduction, by an aluminium or copper chloride reduction, or by a KCl/KF salt melt. Each step loses yield, which is why an ore shortage shows up in capacitor prices months after the mining news.

facts.label: Digestion
facts.value: HF in an autoclave at ~100-200 C

facts.label: Reduction routes
facts.value: Na reduction, Al or Cu reduction, or KCl/KF salt melt

children.note: The brief's chemistry is the standard industrial route and I am reasonably confident in it, but I have compressed several genuinely distinct flows into one node rather than over-claim which variant a given capacitor maker used.

children.name: Columbite-tantalite ore
children.description: The tantalum-bearing ore, a solid solution of columbite and tantalite, mined both as placer gravels and as lode pegmatites. Concentrating it requires ore dressing by gravity and magnetic separation, because only a few per cent of the rock is Ta2O5. Historically the ore was concentrated from the Congo and Rwanda-Burundi, which is precisely why Western capacitor supply chains were politically and economically exposed in this period.
children.note: The DRC ore became a headline conflict-mineral story only from the late 1990s; in 1983-84 the problem was ordinary market tightness and price escalation.

children.name: Dressing and concentration
children.description: Columbite-tantalite is run through gravity, magnetic and electrostatic separation and then an acid-leach circuit to recover a concentrate of perhaps a few per cent Ta2O5. Because the ore is bulk low-grade rock, the mining and concentration stage - not the chemistry - is where most of the cost of a tantalum capacitor lives.

facts.label: Concentration methods
facts.value: gravity shaking tables, magnetic separation, electrostatic separation

children.name: Alluvial and pegmatite placer workings
children.description: Tantalum-bearing minerals are dense, so they concentrate naturally in stream and beach placers below any pegmatite outcrop. Much of the 1980s supply was won by artisanal and semi-industrial alluvial mining in the Kivu highlands, which is exactly why ore supply could be disrupted by regional politics rather than by mine closure.

children.name: Ceramic disc (monolithic disc) capacitor
children.description: A single fired barium-titanate disc with silver electrodes fired onto its two faces. Enormous capacitance for its size and very cheap, but microphonically noisy, temperature-drifty and physically large, with no self-cancelling inductance. On C64 boards of this era the small 0.1 uF parts were already largely the multilayer form.

facts.label: Electrodes
facts.value: silver paste screen-printed and fired on

facts.label: Breakdown
facts.value: ~2.5 kV per um of effective dielectric thickness (design guideline)

facts.label: Weakness
facts.value: resonant above a few MHz; large body

children.name: Pressing, sintering and silver-firing
children.description: BaTiO3 powder is pressed into a disc, sintered at 1200-1300 C, then silver electrode paste is screen-printed onto each face and fired at 700-850 C so the silver is glass-bonded to the ceramic. Only two electrodes exist, so the part cannot cancel its own inductance - the structural reason a disc is useless at radio frequencies and a multilayer is not.

children.name: Disc press and sinter
children.description: A mechanical or hydraulic press blanks the disc to a controlled thickness; the sinter then densifies it and fires on the silver electrodes.

children.name: Disc body material
children.description: The ceramic body of a high-K disc is a modified barium titanate with a glass phase, on an alumina or steatite base. The dielectric-strength figure of about 2.5 kV per micron of effective thickness is a design guideline for the ceramic, not for the finished part.

children.name: Steatite or alumina base
children.description: Low-firing ceramic substrates, steatite (magnesium silicate) or alumina, onto which the high-K layer is applied. Steatite is cheap and fires low; alumina is tougher and better at heat.

children.name: Silica sand
children.description: Quartz sand, the feedstock for glass, for frits and glazes, and for the hydrothermal growth of synthetic quartz. Dredged from beaches or quarried from ancient dune deposits.

children.name: Film capacitors (polyester / polystyrene)
children.description: Film capacitors use a thin metallised plastic film as the dielectric. Non-polar, stable, and tolerant of voltage and temperature excursions. The C64 uses polyester (Melinex/PET) for coupling and decoupling in the analogue paths; polystyrene appears in the precision timing networks of the same era's equipment.

facts.label: Metallisation
facts.value: vacuum-deposited aluminium or zinc on the film

children.name: Vacuum-metallised polyester film
children.description: PET pellets are extruded into a cast film, then stretched fast in two perpendicular directions to several times their original length, orienting the polymer chains. That gives a very thin, very uniform, high-tensile dielectric; then a sub-micron metal layer is vacuum-deposited on one or both faces and the metallised film is wound on a core. No separate foil is used - the electrode IS the deposited layer.
children.note: Metallised film was the volume construction in 1982; separate-foil (film plus separate metal foil) was used for higher-voltage parts.

children.name: PET polymerisation
children.description: The film base is polyethylene terephthalate, made by condensing bis(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate - itself from ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid - in a melt polymeriser at ~250-290 C under vacuum. The terephthalic acid came from paraxylene, which came from the aromatics fraction of a steam cracker or a catalytic reformer.

facts.label: Polymerisation
facts.value: melt condensation at ~270 C under vacuum

children.name: Paraxylene from a steam cracker
children.description: Paraxylene sits in the aromatics complex of a large refinery, separated from a mixed xylene fraction by fractional distillation and adsorption. It is the pivot molecule of the entire polyester industry: 1982 saw PET moving from bottle-grade into film, fibre and capacitor dielectric at once.
children.note: The refining chain belongs to the fluids and chemicals files.

children.name: Polystyrene film capacitor
children.description: A polystyrene dielectric: exceptionally stable, very low dielectric absorption and low loss, historically the timing capacitor of choice for precision RC oscillators before polystyrene's poor mechanical behaviour pushed it into disfavour. Used in analogue equipment of the era, but not a significant part on the C64 mainboard.
children.note: Included to complete the film family; I could not confirm polystyrene parts on a 250407.

facts.label: Dielectric
facts.value: polystyrene, very low loss, very stable

children.name: Styrene polymerisation to polystyrene
children.description: Free-radical or ionic polymerisation of styrene, in bulk suspension or emulsion, gives the amorphous thermoplastic. Unmodified polystyrene is brittle and has poor moisture resistance, which is precisely why metalised polystyrene was restricted to sealed precision parts and lost out to polypropylene.

children.name: Benzene from a steam cracker
children.description: Aromatic hydrocarbon recovered from the aromatics complex of a large cracker or from catalytic reforming of naphtha. The root of styrene, phenol, cumene, aniline and bisphenol.

children.name: Vacuum metallisation of PS film
children.description: The same vacuum-deposited aluminium electrode as on the polyester film, but on a more delicate substrate: polystyrene outgasses and embrittles under vacuum heat, so the film has to be baked and the deposition kept cool.

children.name: Mica capacitor
children.description: A capacitor built from thin sheets of natural muscovite mica with vacuum-deposited aluminium or silver counter-electrodes. Superb temperature stability and high dielectric strength, too expensive and too fragile for general use, so mica was reserved for precision and high-voltage niches in equipment of the era.
