children.note: Mica was being displaced by film and ceramic in mass-market consumer boards by the 1980s; the sputtered metal-insulator-metal mica construction the brief describes is a later, higher-reliability form.

children.name: Muscovite mica, heat-split into sheets
children.description: Natural muscovite is mined in large crystal books from pegmatites and delaminated by heating and cementing against a hot plate, so it splits along its perfect basal cleavage into micrometre-thick, optically flat sheets. The crystal's naturally layered atomic structure gives a very uniform, very thin, very stable dielectric when split this way.

children.name: Pegmatite host rock
children.description: Mica books grow in the giant granitic pegmatites of the Precambrian shield - Minas Gerais in Brazil, Rajasthan in India, Madagascar, and in the United States the Appalachian and Spruce Pine districts of North Carolina. It is mined in situ and split, not manufactured.

children.name: Underground mica mining
children.description: Mica books are followed underground and extracted by hand; the deposit has to be worked selectively because the surrounding pegmatite has to stay intact. Brazilian, Indian and US districts all supply capacitor-grade mica.

children.name: Block and thin grading
children.description: Mica is traded in sizes: block for the thickest uses, thins for splitting, and capacitor mica is the thin and flexible sheet. Grading and splitting, not mining, account for most of the value in the material.

children.name: Heat-and-cement splitting and ruby splitting
children.description: A mica book is mounted on a hot plate; a hot blade of mica is pressed onto it with a cement stick, which drives a wedge along the perfect basal cleavage and peels off a sheet a few microns thick. Repeated, it yields hundreds of optically flat sheets from one crystal, and it is the labour-intensive step that made mica capacitors expensive.
children.note: Splitting is done by hand against a hot plate; automation did not reach the industry in this period.

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: thousands of sheets per cubic foot of rough

children.name: Hot knife and cement stick
children.description: A heated mica blade driven by a cement stick along the cleavage plane. The blade has to be hot enough to part the sheets without charring the cement, and both blade and stick are specialist consumables of the splitting trade.

children.name: Vacuum-deposited counter-electrodes
children.description: Aluminium or silver is evaporated or sputtered through a shadow-mask onto the mica sheets; sheets are stacked with a thin metallised layer between each, bonded under heat and pressure, and the stack is diced into individual capacitors.

facts.label: Deposition
facts.value: vacuum evaporation or sputtering through a shadow mask

children.note: Vacuum evaporation was the 1982 technique; reactive sputtering of a dielectric was the later MIM form.

children.name: Aluminium electrode evaporation
children.description: Aluminium is evaporated rather than sputtered because it is cheap and vapourises at a manageable temperature; it is then left unoxidised under vacuum. Silver electrodes were used where the highest capacitance per unit area was needed.

children.name: Alumina from bauxite
children.description: Smelter-grade alumina, 99.5-99.7 % Al2O3, from the Bayer process. The substrate material for ceramic discs and MLCCs, the can material for resistors, and the dielectric feedstock for the barium titanate chain.

children.name: Bauxite profile
children.description: A soft, deeply weathered tropical profile of hydrated aluminium oxides; mined in open pits, often a few tens of metres thick, sitting directly on the aluminous bedrock.

children.name: Trimmer and variable capacitors
children.description: Small adjustable capacitors used to compensate or trim a circuit. On C64-family boards a trimmer capacitor sits in the crystal oscillator's load network, pulling the frequency exactly onto the NTSC or PAL colour subcarrier; later Commodore boards replaced the earlier adjustable resistor with this capacitor trim.

facts.label: Range
facts.value: a few pF to tens of pF

facts.label: Function
facts.value: crystal load-network trim; swapped in for R27 on later boards

children.name: Air-gap / film trimmer capacitor
children.description: Two sets of interdigitated metal plates with an adjustable overlap, separated by air or a thin film. Turning the screw changes the overlap and therefore the capacitance continuously, letting the factory trim the oscillator to the exact subcarrier frequency. The dielectric is air, which is why these parts are stable and non-drifting.

facts.label: Construction
facts.value: interdigitated plates, air or film dielectric

children.note: The exact trim capacitor reference designator on the 250407 is uncertain to me; the service manual confirms R27 is the adjustable resistor and the later boards use a capacitive trim in the same role.

children.name: Stator and rotor plates
children.description: The trimmer's rotor is a small disc of alumina ceramic, silver-metallised on one face through a spiral or interdigitated pattern. Turning the screw rotates the disc against a fixed plate, so the overlapping metallised area - and hence the capacitance - changes continuously.

facts.label: Dielectric
facts.value: alumina ceramic with a silver counter-electrode, air gap

children.name: Alumina rotor plate material
children.description: The rotor disc is alumina, polished and metallised with a spiral or interdigitated silver pattern. Alumina is used because it is dimensionally stable, machinable to a fine finish and a good insulator at the trimmer's working voltage.

children.name: Alumina from bauxite
children.description: Smelter-grade alumina, 99.5-99.7 % Al2O3, from the Bayer process. The substrate material for ceramic discs and MLCCs, the can material for resistors, and the dielectric feedstock for the barium titanate chain.

children.name: Bauxite profile
children.description: A soft, deeply weathered tropical profile of hydrated aluminium oxides; mined in open pits, often a few tens of metres thick, sitting directly on the aluminous bedrock.

children.name: Capacitor wrap, sleeving and marking
children.description: Not a separate component but the packaging shared across the capacitor families: dipped epoxy for ceramic disc and monolithic parts, printed PVC or polyester sleeving for film caps, cardboard or aluminium sleeves for electrolytics, and printed value/brand markings on all of them.
children.note: The brief asked for the plastic film/foil wrap; that is covered here for the ceramic and film parts, and under alu-electrolytic.assembly for the electrolytics.

children.name: E dipped conformal coat
children.description: Ceramic and monolithic parts were dip-coated in epoxy or PVC after firing to seal the porous body and to carry the printed marking. A dipped part looks identical to a moulded one, which is why it is hard to tell from a photograph whether a given C64 ceramic is disc or monolithic.

children.name: Dip-coating line
children.description: Parts on a wire rack are dipped in an epoxy or PVC solution and withdrawn so the coating tapers at both ends, leaving a characteristic tapered shoulder at the lead exit. A second dip gives the second shoulder.

children.name: Capacitor value marking ink
children.description: Values were printed on the sleeve or dipped coat in an oil-based or epoxy ink on an offset or screen coater. The two-digit and three-digit codes (104 for 100 nF, 104K5V) only became an industry standard in the 1970s.

children.name: Ink pigment
children.description: The value marking pigment is carbon black for dark parts and azo or phthalocyanine colour for bright ones, in a resin vehicle that will not be attacked by the board cleaning solvents.

children.name: Furnace black for the ink
children.description: The same petroleum-derived carbon black as in the resistor body and the rubber dome, ground fine enough to print.

children.name: Printed PVC sleeve on film caps
children.description: Film capacitors arrived in a printed plastic sleeve printed with the value, the rating and the maker. Sleeve polymer is the same PVC family as the case and the cable jacket.

roots.name: Master clock crystal and oscillator
roots.description: Y1, a hermetically sealed HC-49/U quartz crystal, plus the four glue-logic chips that turn it into the machine's entire timing reference: a colour subcarrier crystal oscillator, a PLL that quadruples it, a divider chain, and a phase/frequency detector that locks the dot clock to the colour clock. Every clock edge in a C64 descends from this one 11 mm metal can.
roots.note: IMPORTANT CORRECTION to the brief: the C64 master crystal is NOT 2 MHz or 3.5 MHz. On the NTSC breadbin (ASSY 250407) Y1 is 14.31818 MHz - 6x the NTSC colour subcarrier - and U31's first VCO multiplies it by four in the PLL to give an 8.1818 MHz dot clock, which U30 (74LS193) divides by 7 to 1.16883 MHz, which U29 (74LS74) halves to the 1.022727 MHz Phi 2 CPU clock. The '2 MHz' in Commodore's own service manual is the approximate output of the divider, not the crystal. The PAL crystal is 17.734475 MHz (4x PAL subcarrier); later C64B/C boards used a 16 MHz crystal with a dedicated clock-generator IC.

children.name: Y1 quartz crystal, HC-49/U
children.description: A plano-convex quartz plate, 0.07 mm thick, with electrodes fired on its two faces, held on supports inside a small metal can filled with argon and sealed by a crimped, resistance-welded cap. The quartz is the oscillator's frequency-setting element: the whole machine's timing accuracy is the accuracy of one cut and lapped slice of Brazilian or synthetic silicon dioxide.

facts.label: Frequency stability
facts.value: roughly +/-0.01 % over 0-50 C for a good AT-cut part

facts.label: Load
facts.value: ~30 pF CL in a Pierce oscillator

facts.label: Fill gas
facts.value: argon or krypton at a few kPa

children.name: Natural rock crystal (Brazilian quartz)
children.description: Gem-quality clear quartz for crystal units came historically from the rock-crystal veins of Minas Gerais in Brazil, prized for natural faces that need no lapping and for the very low defect density that makes a low-phase-noise oscillator possible. By the early 1980s this was being displaced by hydrothermal synthetic quartz, which is chemically identical and far more uniform.

children.name: Quartz vein in pegmatite host
children.description: Clear quartz crystallises in the pockets and miarolitic cavities of granitic pegmatite, growing inward from the cavity walls until the void is filled - which is why Brazilian rock crystal comes out with flat crystal faces already in place. Mined by hand-scale underground workings and by washing decomposed pegmatite.

children.name: Granite pegmatite body
children.description: A late-stage, volatile-rich, very coarse-grained intrusive igneous rock: quartz, K-feldspar, muscovite and tourmaline in crystals up to many centimetres across. Pegmatites are the pegmatite-parental source of both quartz and mica on this tree.

children.name: Pegmatite completion
children.description: The last melt water of a granite intrusion concentrates volatiles into a very coarse, quartz-rich final stage. Rock crystal and mica are two products of the same geology, which is why both appear in this tree from the same kind of ground.

children.name: Hand mining of rock crystal
children.description: Brazilian rock crystal was worked in small underground operations following the vein, split out and sold as it was found. It was never a large-tonnage commodity, which is part of why synthetic quartz took over so decisively.

children.name: Hydrothermal synthetic quartz
children.description: Because natural quartz is limited and variable, industry moved to growing it: an autoclave is charged with silica (often crushed natural quartz) in a hot sodium-hydroxide solution and heated at around 400 C and 150 MPa. Quartz grows on seed crystals hung in the solution, growing the rough in days rather than geological time. This is the source of nearly all quartz crystal blanks made from about the mid-1970s onward.

children.name: Steel autoclave with seed crystals
children.description: A filled, sealed pressure vessel - usually Hastelloy or 17-4PH steel liner - held at high temperature and pressure so an alkaline solution dissolves silica from the feed and re-deposits it on zoned seed crystals. Temperature gradients create the supersaturation that drives growth; the growth zones themselves are what later become the tuned crystal's resonators.
children.note: The brief cites NaOH at 400 C and 150 MPa; both alkali routes were used, KOH predominating for the highest-purity synthetic growth.

children.name: Alkali solvent
children.description: The growth solution is hot concentrated sodium or potassium hydroxide, which dissolves silica at the elevated temperature while quartz re-deposits on the seeds. The alkali is made from chlor-alkali electrolysis of brine - so the crystal ultimately touches rock salt as well as quartz sand.

children.name: Rock salt / brine
children.description: Halite, mined or solution-mined, and the source of the chlorine and sodium that make the caustic soda that seeds the quartz growth. A surprising number of industrial processes begin at a salt mine.

children.name: Seed crystals and zoning
children.description: Growth happens on thin zoned seed plates hung in the vessel, and the growth itself develops the acoustic zoning structure that later becomes the crystal's resonators. This is why synthetic quartz, not natural quartz, is what nearly every 1982 crystal was grown from.

children.name: Quartz sand / crushed quartz feed
children.description: The silica feedstock for the autoclave is cleaned quartz sand or lumps of milky quartz. Natural quartz sand is a common beach and dune sand: essentially SiO2, left behind as quartz survives weathering while everything else dissolves and washes away.

children.name: Quartz sand, SiO2
children.description: The most abundant framework silicate in continental crust. Weathering destroys feldspar and ferromagnesian minerals and leaves a residue of quartz grains, which are worked by screening and magnetic separation into glass sand, foundry sand and ceramic-grade sand.

children.name: Sawing, lapping and X-ray orienting the blank
children.description: Rough crystal is sawn into blanks, then the cut face is lapped to about 0.15 mm and X-ray diffracted to find its crystallographic orientation. Orientation is everything: only an AT-cut at the right angle gives the flat temperature curve a frequency-stable oscillator needs.

facts.label: Orientation
facts.value: X-ray diffractometer; AT-cut ~35 deg to the X axis for 1980s units

children.name: X-ray orientation and AT-cut angle selection
children.description: A synthetic rough is indexed by X-ray diffraction so its Z axis and X axis are known, then sawn at a chosen angle to the X axis (the 'AT-cut'). The mid-1980s standard for general-purpose oscillators was about 35 degrees; this angle is chosen because it lands the resonance on a flat, temperature-insensitive point in the quartz stiffness-temperature curve.

facts.label: Instrument
facts.value: four-circle X-ray diffractometer with a goniometer

children.name: Lapping and double-lap polishing
children.description: The cut blank is lapped on rotating cast-iron plates with progressively finer abrasives (aluminium oxide, then colloidal silica) down to about 0.15 mm, then double-lapped against a second plate to remove bow and damage left by the saw. Crystal blanks for a 1982 oscillator were lapped on plates run by lapidary and lapping shops, not in the same plant that makes the finished crystal.

children.name: Final lapping abrasive
children.description: The last lapping stage uses a colloidal silica slurry, which polishes rather than cuts. Colloidal silica is precipitated from a dilute sodium silicate solution, itself made from silica sand and sodium carbonate.

children.name: Silica sand for the sodium silicate
children.description: Quartz sand fused with sodium carbonate makes the water glass that the colloidal silica is precipitated from.

children.name: Grinding the lens shape
children.description: The face is bevelled and the outline ground so the finished blank is a lens or plano-convex dome rather than a flat slab. The convexity is deliberate: it makes the crystal's resonant frequency less sensitive to surface damage and to where the mounting points press on it.

facts.label: Final plate thickness
facts.value: ~0.07 mm at the centre, bevelled to ~0.1 mm at the edge

facts.label: Why bevelled
facts.value: so the supports never touch the vibrating centre

children.name: Mounting and soldering of the crystal
children.description: The four HC-49 leads are formed to a right angle and soldered onto the board in a wave-solder pass. The crystal's case sits at the board's natural mechanical frequency well below the circuit's operating frequency, which is deliberate: an HC-49 body has several overtone resonances that would otherwise produce spurious oscillator modes.

children.name: Formed leads
children.description: The four flat HC-49 leads are bent to a right angle and trimmed, then soldered onto the board. The case is deliberately stood off the board so air can move around it, because the case's own overtone resonances must sit well below the operating frequency.

children.name: Diamond grinding wheel
children.description: A resin-bonded diamond wheel, used wet, that bevels the plate edge and cuts the lens curvature. In 1982 diamond abrasive was largely synthetic, made from graphite under a shock wave; natural diamond was reserved for dressing the wheels.

children.name: Graphite precursor of synthetic diamond
children.description: Explosion-wave synthesis of diamond is fed with graphite, itself made from petroleum coke calcined at ~3000 C in an Acheson furnace. So even the abrasive that cuts the crystal descends from petroleum coke.
children.note: Natural flake graphite was also used; the Acheson petroleum-coke route dominated synthetic production in 1982.

children.name: Frequency grinding
children.description: The final grinding is done with the plate already oscillating in a test jig: the grinder watches the frequency change as material is removed and stops at the target. This is why a crystal can be hit to within a few hertz before it is even put into its can.

children.name: Metal electrodes on the blank faces
children.description: Chromium is evaporated or sputtered onto both faces as an adhesion layer, then gold or silver is deposited over it as the conductive electrode, through a shadow mask that defines the electrode area. Chromium-gold is the classic 1980s crystal electrode stack: Cr to bond, Au to conduct.

facts.label: Pattern
facts.value: shadow-mask defined, 6-14 mm2 for a 1982 HC-49

children.note: Some 1980s HC-49/U crystals used nickel electrodes over chromium for economy; gold-over-chromium was the higher-reliability standard.

children.name: Chromium adhesion layer
children.description: Chromium is evaporated as the adhesion layer because bare quartz will not hold gold by van der Waals forces alone. Chromium wets both the quartz surface and the gold film, and it is itself a hard, chemically inert metal.

children.name: Chromium (chromite) for the adhesion layer
children.description: The chromium in a crystal electrode is a small mass but it is ordinary metallurgical chromium, and chromite ore from the Bushveld Complex is the source.

children.name: Gold electrode film
children.description: Gold evaporated through a shadow mask to give the electrode its final geometry and conductivity. The mask pattern fixes the electrode area, which together with the plate thickness is what sets the crystal capacitance.

children.name: Evaporation shadow mask
children.description: A thin metal mask placed above the rotating blank during evaporation so the electrode pattern is defined. The mask is made from a drawn stainless or nickel strip, chemically etched to the electrode shape.

children.name: Cutting the plate and vacuum baking
children.description: The plated blank is cut with a diamond wheel into individual resonator plates, then the plates are vacuum-baked at around 400 C to drive off adsorbed moisture and contaminants. That vacuum bake is what removes the piezoelectric pyroelectric drift and the 'dope' effect - the stress-induced frequency shift as a crystal heats - and it is why a crystal that has been opened is never a good crystal.

facts.label: Consequence
facts.value: good level frequency stability over temperature

children.name: Diamond dicing saw
children.description: A thin resin-bonded diamond wheel, ~0.03-0.05 mm thick, cutting the plated blank into resonators. The wheel has to be extremely thin and extremely flat to avoid chipping a 0.07 mm plate.

children.name: Cleaning between steps
children.description: Every step from lapping onward is done washed and clean: a fingerprint on a 0.07 mm plate changes the frequency. Crystal preparation is one of the few wet, cold, dirty-looking processes in electronics.

children.name: Deionised rinse water
children.description: Every crystal process rinse uses deionised water, because a single dissolved ion on a resonating plate changes the frequency measurably. City water is nowhere good enough.

children.name: Ion-exchange resin
children.description: A cation and an anion resin pair in two columns, regenerated with acid and alkali, removes the dissolved ions. The resin is a cross-linked polystyrene with sulfonic or quaternary ammonium groups.

children.name: HC-49/U case: crimp, weld and argon fill
children.description: The plate sits on a pair of wire supports in a crimped and welded nickel can, filled with argon or krypton at a few kPa. The can is drawn from nickel-plated steel or brass, and its small welded lid is what makes the unit hermetic - the reason a 1982 crystal does not drift as the humidity of an attic changes.

facts.label: Case
facts.value: HC-49/U, ~11 x 4.5 x 3.5 mm, four leads

facts.label: Fill gas
facts.value: argon or krypton at a few kPa

facts.label: Seal
facts.value: crimped collar plus a spot-welded / resistance-welded lid

facts.label: Supports
facts.value: spring wire mounts holding the plate at the stress-minimising points

children.name: Nickel can stock
children.description: HC-49/U cans were drawn from nickel or nickel-plated strip steel, or from brass with a nickel finish. Nickel is used because it matches the thermal expansion of the quartz and the electrode leads closely enough that the mounting stress does not drift the frequency.
children.note: The nickel feed chain itself is not traced here; the interconnect file covers nickel plating.

children.name: Drawn can stock
children.description: The HC-49/U can is deep-drawn from thin nickel-plated strip in a progressive tool, then the crimped collar is rolled and the lid welded on. Both operations happen before the plate goes in - the can is made empty and loaded later.

children.name: Welded lid and crimped collar
children.description: The lid is spot-welded or resistance-welded to the collar in an atmosphere of dry hydrogen or forming gas, which keeps the internal oxide clean and lets the fill gas stay inert. Hermeticity is what makes a forty-year-old crystal hold its frequency.

children.name: Forming gas for welding
children.description: A mixture of hydrogen and nitrogen used as a cover during the lid weld. Hydrogen also diffuses any internal oxide onto the getters, which is why a well-made can can have a getter mirror at the bottom after opening.

children.name: Argon or krypton fill gas
children.description: The can is filled with a chemically inert gas before welding. Argon is preferred because it does not react with the electrode and cannot outgas; krypton was used where a slightly more hermetic atmosphere was wanted. The gas also damps acoustic vibration in the plate.

children.name: Cryogenic air separation
children.description: Argon and krypton are separated from liquefied air by fractional distillation at around 90 K in a double-column distiller. Every quartz crystal can on earth is filled with gas that was once part of the atmosphere, separated cryogenically.

facts.label: Argon cut point
facts.value: ~-185 C boiling point region in the argon-oxygen column

children.name: Spring-wire supports
children.description: Two short wires spot-welded to the plate's major faces at the nodal points. Because quartz is piezoelectric, mechanically stressing it shifts its resonant frequency, so the supports must sit where the strain of the vibrating mode is smallest - the whole reason the plate is bevelled and domed.

facts.label: Position
facts.value: the mechanical nodal points of the resonating mode

facts.label: Material
facts.value: gold or nickel wire, spot-welded to the electrodes

children.name: Gold or nickel support wire
children.description: Fine wire, 0.1-0.2 mm, spot-welded to the plate electrodes. Gold is preferred where maximum Q is needed; nickel is the cost-driven choice for the volume 1982 HC-49.

children.name: Oscillator and PLL circuitry
children.description: The crystal is only the frequency reference. Turning it into the machine's clocks takes a 74LS629 dual VCO crystal oscillator, a Motorola MC4044 phase/frequency detector, a 74LS193 divider, and a 74LS74 flip-flop, with R27 or a trimmer capacitor setting the exact pull.
children.note: These four are logic ICs rather than passives, but they belong in this branch because without them the quartz is inert. Their fabrication is out of scope for this file.

facts.label: Oscillator topology
facts.value: Pierce (series-mode) in the 74LS629's crystal oscillator half

facts.label: Trim
facts.value: R27 500 ohm cermet trimmer on early boards, capacitive trim on later

facts.label: PLL
facts.value: MC4044 drives the 74LS629's VCO control pin, locking the dot clock to 4x the colour clock

children.name: Pierce oscillator and load capacitors
children.description: The crystal acts as a negative-resistance element in a Pierce oscillator with a small load capacitor at its CL, and the drive level set by a series resistor. The load capacitors and the trim element together decide the frequency pull range; this is why the crystal's specified CL (typically about 30 pF in an HC-49/U) has to be matched by the board.

facts.label: Drive level
facts.value: tens of microwatts (mA-scale drive in the 74LS629)

children.note: The discrete load caps are ceramic (see mb.passives.caps.trim and the C0G timing caps); a Pierce oscillator's frequency is very sensitive to stray capacitance, which is why the C64 needed an adjustable trim.

children.name: Load capacitors and stray capacitance
children.description: The Pierce oscillator's frequency is set by the crystal's CL, the load capacitors and the transistor's input capacitance all in series. At 14 MHz with a few tens of picofarads involved, a 0.5 mm of stray copper changes the trim range - which is why the C64 needed an adjustable element here rather than a fixed capacitor.

children.name: Load capacitor type and value
children.description: A small ceramic part, chosen with a tight tolerance because its value enters the oscillator directly. On the C64 this is where the C0G-grade ceramic timing caps are used, and where the trim element sits.

children.name: Alumina from bauxite
children.description: Smelter-grade alumina, 99.5-99.7 % Al2O3, from the Bayer process. The substrate material for ceramic discs and MLCCs, the can material for resistors, and the dielectric feedstock for the barium titanate chain.

children.name: Bauxite profile
children.description: A soft, deeply weathered tropical profile of hydrated aluminium oxides; mined in open pits, often a few tens of metres thick, sitting directly on the aluminous bedrock.

children.name: Oscillator startup and drive level
children.description: The oscillator is a high-gain positive-feedback amplifier at all frequencies until the crystal's impedance peaks at the design frequency. The circuit is designed to start on noise and settle; a badly driven crystal never settles, which is the classic symptom of a crystal with a cracked plate.

children.name: PLL: MC4044 into the 74LS629 VCO
children.description: The 74LS629's second oscillator is a voltage-controlled oscillator. The MC4044 phase/frequency detector compares a divided colour clock against the VIC-II's phase-0 clock and returns a DC control voltage on pin 8, which the 74LS629's frequency-control pin steers. That is the whole of the C64's PLL: a crystal oscillator for the exact subcarrier, and a tracking VCO four times faster, locked to it, for the pixel clock.

children.name: Why a trim is required at all
children.description: The NTSC colour subcarrier is specified to about 5 parts in 10^7, and an untrimmed crystal and oscillator would wander far more than that over temperature and supply. The trim element (R27 on breadbin boards, a capacitive trim later) lets the whole PLL be pulled onto the exact frequency at the factory and then holds it there.

children.name: PAL and NTSC crystals
children.description: The PAL machine uses a 17.734475 MHz crystal (four times the 4.433619 MHz PAL subcarrier) in the same circuit, and the 74LS193 divider is switched to divide by nine instead of seven. Later C64B/C boards moved to a 16 MHz crystal and a dedicated clock-generator IC, dropping the discrete VCO.

roots.name: Switches and slide potentiometers
roots.description: Three human-operated controls on a C64: the mains-free power slider SW1 on the right-hand case panel, and the two slide potentiometers for volume/tone and brightness on the top surface. The power switch gates the incoming 5 V rail; the two potentiometers are wired directly into the SID audio output and the VIC-II's analogue video level.

facts.label: SW1 position
facts.value: right-hand case panel, between the control ports and the power socket

facts.label: Type
facts.value: single-pole slide switch, SPST, mains-rated style body

facts.label: Potentiometers
facts.value: 2 x miniature slide potentiometer, ~10 kOhm linear

facts.label: Slider location
facts.value: top surface of the case, right-hand end

children.name: SW1 power slider switch
children.description: A single-pole, double-throw or single-throw slide switch on the mainboard, actuated by a moulded slider that protrudes through a rectangular cut-out in the right-hand side of the case. Its only job in the C64 is to interrupt the incoming +5 V rail - everything else on the board runs off the switch's output side.

facts.label: Rating
facts.value: ~6 A at 250 VAC resistive, far beyond the C64's ~1 A load

children.name: Moulded switch body (melamine / phenolic / nylon)
children.description: The insulator the whole mechanism lives in. Small slide switches of this generation used a filled thermoset (melamine-formaldehyde or glass-filled phenolic) or a glass-filled nylon; both mould well in simple two-plate tools and stand a soldering iron's heat. Melamine was the industry default because its arc resistance in a mains-adjacent switch is better than polystyrene's.
children.note: The C64 switch handles only 5 V DC from the external brick, not mains, so its insulation requirement was modest - but the part was bought from a mains-switch catalogue and over-specified.

children.name: Melamine-formaldehyde thermoset
children.description: A thermoset built from melamine and formaldehyde, filled with cellulose or glass fibre, and compression-moulded hot. It is rigid, arc-resistant, dimensionally stable and cheap - the standard insulator for mains switches and domestic electrical accessories of the period.

children.name: Melamine resin from urea and formaldehyde
children.description: Melamine is made by condensing urea with formaldehyde. Urea comes from ammonia and carbon dioxide, both cheap industrial gases; formaldehyde comes from oxidising methanol, which comes from the catalytic conversion of synthesis gas. Both halves were pure petrochemical by 1982.

facts.label: Formaldehyde route
facts.value: methanol from CO/H2, silver-catalysed oxidation to formaldehyde

children.name: Glass-filled nylon (PA66-GF)
children.description: A tough, self-lubricating engineering thermoplastic used where a moving slider needs low friction and good wear resistance against the moulded track. Injection-moulded into the actuator and often into the switch's own guide body.
children.note: Which of these the C64's switch actually used is not documented anywhere I could find; the materials above are the standard options for a 1982 miniature slide switch.

children.name: Glass filler in the nylon
children.description: 30 % chopped glass fibre in the PA66, for stiffness at a thin wall and for dimensional stability against the moulded detent. The same filler as in the connector housings.

children.name: Nylon-6-6 polymer (caprolactam)
children.description: The base polymer of PA66, made by hydrolytic ring-opening polymerisation of caprolactam, itself made from benzene via phenol and cyclohexanone. It replaced silk and nylon-6 for mechanical parts because of its moisture stability and higher melting point.
children.note: The petrochemical chain from benzene to caprolactam to nylon-6-6 is real 1980s chemistry but is not expanded here; it belongs in the plastics file.

children.name: Caprolactam to nylon-6-6
children.description: Caprolactam is polymerised hydrolytically, or converted to the salt and polymerised as a nylon salt, in a continuous process at ~250-280 C. The caprolactam itself comes from phenol or cyclohexanone - both benzene derivatives from a steam cracker or catalytic reformer.

children.name: Benzene from the cracker
children.description: Benzene is one of the oldest commercially useful petrochemicals: it was isolated from coal tar long before 1982, but by then most industrial benzene came from the aromatics complex of a steam cracker, made by catalytic reforming of naphtha. It is the root of the styrene, phenol, nylon and epoxy trees.

children.name: Solder terminals and anchor
children.description: The pins of the switch are brass, either solid or a brass tube over a steel mandrel with a solder tail. Brass is used because it wets tin-lead solder reliably and does not need nickel underplate for a low-voltage contact.

children.name: Brass pin stock
children.description: Solid brass wire or a brass tube over a steel mandrel, cut and headed. Brass is chosen because it is springy enough to survive the assembly line and soft enough to take a solder joint.

children.name: Case screws and panel mounting
children.description: The switch body was riveted or snapped into the mainboard and located by the case's moulded boss. The moulded boss and its snap feature are part of the case tooling, not the switch tooling.

children.name: Slide mechanism, actuator and detent
children.description: The actuator is a moulded slider with ribs that engage moulded detent ramps in the body, so it clicks into a definite position at each end rather than resting ambiguously. A moulded spring or a bent leaf spring inside supplies the return force and the over-centre snap that gives the switch its tactile 'click'.
children.note: The detent geometry (moulded ramp plus leaf spring) is standard 1980s miniature-switch practice; I have no teardown-level measurement of the specific C64 switch.

children.name: Return leaf spring
children.description: A bent spring steel leaf that provides the over-centre force and the return to OFF. It is the part that fatigues: after enough actuations it loses tension and the switch no longer snaps crisply.

children.name: Spring steel strip
children.description: A high-carbon strip steel, hardened and tempered, cut and blanked. Blade and coil spring steel of this quality came from the same integrated steel plants as the razor blades and the automotive leaf springs.

children.name: Moulded detent ramp
children.description: A stepped ramp moulded into the nylon body or actuator over which the slider rides, giving a definite position at each end. Moulding the detent rather than machining it is what keeps the part cheap at the volumes a consumer switch sold in.

children.name: Leaf contacts and contact plating
children.description: A pair of formed leaf springs - phosphor bronze or stainless - carry the current; one is fixed and one moves with the slider, wiping against its mate over a small spring pressure so the electrical contact area is always fresh. The wipe is the whole reason slide switches do not corrode: an oxide film is continuously displaced.

facts.label: Contact plating
facts.value: silver, silver-nickel, or a gold flash for low-level signals

facts.label: Contact pressure
facts.value: tens to hundreds of grams per contact

children.note: For a 5 V DC power switch the plating is silver; the gold-flashed variety was for the low-level contacts of the pots and connectors.

children.name: Phosphor bronze leaf stock
children.description: A copper-tin alloy with a few tenths of a per cent of phosphorus, valued for springiness, fatigue resistance and a low and stable contact resistance. Drawn strip, blanked, pierced and formed in a progressive die; the standard contact alloy of the whole electronics industry.

children.name: Tin in the bronze (from tin ore)
children.description: The tin that makes phosphor bronze springy and corrosion-resistant came from cassiterite, the ore of tin, worked since the Bronze Age and still a major traded commodity in 1982.
children.note: The cassiterite -> tin chain is expanded in the metals file; referenced here only.

children.name: Copper of the bronze (from copper ore)
children.description: Refined from chalcopyrite or native copper, smelted, converted and electrolytically refined, then drawn, rolled and annealed into the contact strip. The same copper, more or less, appears in the C64's traces, connectors and windings.
children.note: The smelter and refinery chain is expanded in the metals file.

children.name: Volume and brightness slide potentiometers
children.description: Two miniature slide potentiometers on the mainboard whose sliders protrude through the top of the case. One sets the audio level at the SID output; the other sets the analogue video brightness level. Both use a printed resistive track and a spring-loaded wiper.
children.note: I could not verify the exact resistance and taper of the two C64 slide pots from a primary source. Contemporary photographs and the schematic suggest a linear-law miniature slide pot in the 1 kOhm-100 kOhm range; treat the value as uncertain.

facts.label: Construction
facts.value: printed carbon track on a ceramic or phenolic substrate

children.name: Printed carbon track on a ceramic substrate
children.description: The resistive element is a track of carbon ink printed onto a flat ceramic or phenolic substrate, with metal end lands at each end. Printing is what makes a slide pot cheap: the geometry of the track, its length and its taper, sets both the total resistance and the law.

facts.label: Ink
facts.value: carbon/graphite in an organic binder, or a cermet (RuO2 + glass) paste

facts.label: Print
facts.value: screen-printed through a mesh, cured in a tunnel oven

facts.label: Substrate
facts.value: flat alumina ceramic or glass-filled phenolic

children.note: A printed carbon track and a printed cermet track are the same manufacturing route as the thick-film resistor networks on the same board; only the geometry differs. For low-level audio pots in 1982, carbon ink on ceramic was still the norm and cermet was the higher-quality option.

children.name: Carbon ink for the printed track
children.description: Carbon black ground into a binder to a printable ink, screen-printed along the substrate and cured in a tunnel oven. The track length sets the nominal resistance and its taper sets the law; the two C64 sliders are linear, so the printed geometry is constant width.

facts.label: Ink
facts.value: carbon black in an organic binder, screen-printed and cured

children.name: Furnace black in the pot track
children.description: The printed track uses a fine carbon black, finely ground so it prints smoothly and fires into a hard conductive film. The same powder, ground finer, is in the resistor film and the rubber dome.

children.name: Substrate and end lands
children.description: The carbon track is printed between two metallic end lands, usually fired silver, one at each end of the travel. The wiper bridges them; the centre terminal taps the wiper. All three terminals are solder pins on the pot's tail.

children.name: Firing of the printed substrate
children.description: The carbon or cermet track is fired into the ceramic substrate in a tunnel oven at several hundred degrees, fusing the binder and the glass frit so the track cannot be scratched off by the wiper.

children.name: Spring-loaded wiper
children.description: A small sprung metal clip or blade, usually a copper-nickel-plated spring steel or nickel strip, presses onto the carbon track and taps the voltage off at whatever point along it the slider has dragged it to. It must carry current through a sliding contact, so its plating and its spring force are the two design limits.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: Ni-plated spring steel, or phosphor bronze

facts.label: Wear
facts.value: the carbon track is deliberately sacrificial - it wears before the wiper

children.note: A worn carbon track is the classic reason a 1980s volume pot develops noise or drops to one end of its travel; contact cleaner and a rebuild pen were the standard fixes.

children.name: Plated spring-steel strip
children.description: The wiper is stamped from spring strip and plated in a nickel or precious-metal bath so that it both springs correctly and carries current across a sliding contact without galling the carbon track.

children.name: Nickel plating bath
children.description: The same nickel chemistry as the resistor lead plating and the connector underplate: a sulfamate or pyrophosphate bath, or electroless nickel-phosphorus where the deposit had to be hard.

children.name: Pre-contact break and noise
children.description: A resistive track and a sliding contact inherently generate noise, and a cheap carbon track generates a lot. C64 volume pots are a well-known source of a faint hiss or crackle in the audio output - a real consequence of the printed-carbon technology, not a fault.

children.name: Moulded housing and slider knob
children.description: A small injection-moulded thermoplastic body with the moulded detent rails for the slider, and a moulded knob with the finger rib that protrudes through the case cut-out. The same polymer families as the switch body: nylon, ABS or a filled phenoxy.
children.note: Polymers and their moulding are expanded in the plastics file.

children.name: Injection moulding of the pot body
children.description: The body is injection moulded with the three terminal slots, the detent rails and the wiper guide all in one shot, in a multi-cavity tool shared with the rest of the world's miniature slide pot production.

children.name: ABS or PBT housing polymer
children.description: Either the same ABS as the keycaps or a glass-filled PBT. Both are chosen for stiffness at a thin wall - a pot body has to hold a wiper alignment over millimetres of travel without creeping.

children.name: Moulded slider knob
children.description: A small moulded knob with a moulded-in guide rib that engages the body's rails, protruding through the case cut-out. The knob and the body were often moulded in the same tool family so the fit is guaranteed.

children.name: ABS for the slider knob
children.description: The knob is ABS because it has to be moulded thin, in a gloss finish, with a fine rib. It is the same polymer as the keycaps a few inches away on the same machine.

children.name: Styrene for the ABS
children.description: The styrene monomer that gives ABS its rigid, gloss-forming phase.

children.name: Benzene from a steam cracker
children.description: Aromatic hydrocarbon recovered from the aromatics complex of a large cracker or from catalytic reforming of naphtha. The root of styrene, phenol, cumene, aniline and bisphenol.

children.name: Single and ganged (twin) sections
children.description: A potentiometer is made in two or three mechanically independent sections that share a common wiper shaft, so one slider knob moves the end terminal, the wiper and the middle terminal together. A 'ganged' pair means two complete potentiometers on one shaft; the C64's two sliders are physically separate parts rather than a ganged pair, since they control completely unrelated signals in different parts of the machine.
children.note: The brief asked about a ganged twin version; the C64 does not use one. Ganging was standard on stereo audio controls, not on the C64.

children.name: Common wiper shaft
children.description: A drawn steel shaft pressed through the moulded wiper carriers, so all the potentiometer sections move together. Drawing the shaft from steel rather than moulding it in plastic is what keeps the alignment over millions of slider cycles.

children.name: Steel for the shaft
children.description: Mild steel drawn bar. The chain from iron ore to drawn bar is the same one behind every other steel part on the machine.

children.name: Self-lubricating bushing
children.description: A moulded nylon or PTFE-impregnated bushing in the chassis that the shaft runs in. Dry, it is what makes a slider pot feel smooth rather than gritty.

children.name: PTFE-impregnated bushing
children.description: A nylon or bronze-impregnated bushing with a PTFE (Teflon) lubricant. PTFE is made by polymerising tetrafluoroethylene, whose monomer is made from fluorspar via hydrofluoric acid and chloroform.

children.name: Fluorspar for the fluorine
children.description: Fluorspar, calcium fluoride, was the world's main source of fluorine for PTFE and refrigerant fluorocarbons. Its acid-grade material was a genuine traded mineral in 1982.

roots.name: Front and rear I/O connectors
roots.description: Every plug-in interface on a C64: the 24-pin user port, the 2x6 cassette port, the 44-pin cartridge socket, the 8-pin DIN video/audio and 6-pin DIN serial connectors, the two DE-9 control ports, the 7-pin PSU inlet and the keyboard ribbon header. They share one manufacturing sequence: stamped-and-formed brass contacts, nickel underplate, gold flash, and an injection-moulded thermoplastic or glass-filled phenolic insulator.
roots.note: CORRECTION to the brief: the breadbin C64 has NO RCA jacks. Composite video, luma, chroma, audio and the RF modulator output all leave through a single round 8-pin DIN connector on the rear panel (an earlier 1982 revision used a 5-pin one); RCA sockets appear on the C64C and on Commodore's own 1701/1702 monitors. The 'DIN-5 cassette port' is also not quite right - the datasette port is a 2x6 card-edge socket on the motherboard, and the DIN plug lives on the datasette cable. The PSU inlet is 7-pin, not 6.

facts.label: User port
facts.value: 24-pin card edge, 3.96 mm pitch, gold over nickel

facts.label: Control ports
facts.value: 2 x DE-9 subminiature D, plastic shell, gold-flashed

facts.label: Keyboard
facts.value: soldered board header at the front-left edge carrying a flat ribbon

children.name: Shared contact manufacturing: stamping, forming, plating
children.description: Almost every connector here is made the same way at the front end: a brass or phosphor-bronze strip is blanked, pierced, bent and formed in a multi-slide tool, then plated in a nickel bath and given a thin gold flash on the contact areas.

children.name: Four-slide die forming (blank, pierce, form, cut)
children.description: Contacts are made on a multi-slide machine: a brass or copper-alloy strip is fed as a continuous coil, and each station in the slide performs one operation - piercing the terminal slot, forming the spring barrel, bending the solder tail, then cutting off the finished contact. Hundreds of thousands of identical contacts per hour, which is why connectors are cheap.

facts.label: Strip
facts.value: ~0.3-0.5 mm thick brass or phosphor bronze

children.note: High-speed stamping of this sort is how a DE-9's dimpled gold-flashed contact costs fractions of a cent.

children.name: Tool steel of the stamping die
children.description: The progressive die is made from hardened tool steel - P20 for the body, D2 or H13 for the cutting edges - with the contact geometry machined and ground. A stamping die outlasts tens of millions of strokes, which is why the contact is a commodity.

children.name: Iron ore behind the die steel
children.description: Tool steel is made in the same integrated plants as everything else: ore to blast furnace to basic oxygen furnace to alloyed bar.

children.name: Coiled contact strip
children.description: The blank comes off the coil as a continuous ribbon of brass strip, the cheapest way to feed a high-speed press. The whole 44-position cartridge socket's 88 contacts are stamped from one coil.

children.name: Copper rod to contact strip
children.description: Brass strip is rolled from drawn copper-tin rod on a Sendimir mill. The copper is refined to cathode, cast to wire rod and drawn; the tin and zinc are added in the melt.

children.name: Copper ore
children.description: Chalcopyrite or native copper, refined and drawn. The chain from ore to contact strip is two or three steps.

children.name: Brass strip (Cu-Zn)
children.description: Cartridge brass, usually 70/30 copper-zinc, drawn into strip. Brass is used because it is easy to form, springs usefully, and takes nickel plating well; a strip's mechanical properties are set by the zinc content and by work hardening from the drawing die.

facts.label: Hard-rolled
facts.value: full hard strip for spring terminals

children.name: Copper of the brass
children.description: Refined from chalcopyrite, mined underground or in porphyry open pits, smelted and then electrorefined to 99.99 % and cast into a wire rod. The same copper appears in the connector shells, the board's traces and the coils of the RF modulator.
children.note: Smelting and refining chain is expanded in the metals file.

children.name: Copper electrorefining
children.description: Blister copper from the smelter is refined electrolytically to 99.99 % cathode, which is then cast to wire rod and rolled into foil. Electrorefining is what makes the uniform, sulphur-free copper that both brass contact strip and solderable connector plating require.

facts.label: By-product
facts.value: anode slime, the main source of silver, selenium and tellurium

children.name: Blister copper from the smelter
children.description: Fire-refined copper at 96-98 % purity, still carrying enough precious metals and impurities to pay for its own electrorefining. Modern smelters in 1982 moved to direct-to-blister continuous casting, cutting the fire-refining step.

children.name: Zinc of the brass
children.description: Zinc is recovered from sphalerite ore, roasted to the oxide and either smelted to crude zinc or leached and electrowon; it is the element that makes copper springy and hard-working.
children.note: The zinc chain belongs to the metals file; referenced here only.

children.name: Sphalerite (zinc blende)
children.description: The dominant zinc ore, usually a cubic sulphide with variable iron content, mined underground in limestone-hosted replacement deposits. Concentrates are roasted to the oxide or leached.

children.name: Roasting and calcination
children.description: The concentrate is fluid-bed roasted, oxidising ZnS to ZnO with SO2 recovered as sulphuric acid. The oxide is then either smelted with coke to crude zinc or leached and electrowon.

children.name: Nickel underplate then gold flash
children.description: Two plating baths in sequence. First a nickel underplate (electroless nickel-phosphorus on some parts, barrel or rack electrolytic nickel on others) is laid down; this is the barrier layer that stops the base copper or brass diffusing into the gold, and nickel is also what the solder actually wets. Then a thin gold flash - typically 0.05-0.5 um over nickel - goes on the mating contact areas only, masked by selective plating or by tabbing the contact.

facts.label: Nickel
facts.value: ~2-5 um; electroless Ni-P ~2-5 um with ~0.3-5 % phosphorus

facts.label: Why gold
facts.value: gold does not oxidise, so the contact resistance stays low forever

facts.label: Why nickel under it
facts.value: nickel is a diffusion barrier; gold on bare copper/alloy would diffuse and flake

children.note: Commodore specified gold-flashed contacts on the user port and cartridge socket; the eBay/C64 spares listings for the 24-pin user-port connector state 'gold over nickel' explicitly. The DE-9 control ports and the DIN connectors were gold-flashed too, though the DIN shells were nickel-plated steel rather than gold.
children.note2: The 'immersion gold / electroless nickel' in the brief is right in kind. Immersion gold (a displacement process, a few tenths of a micron, no current) was used for the flash; electroless nickel was one of the two underplate processes, the other being electrolytic nickel. Both existed in 1982.

children.name: Electroless nickel-phosphorus deposition
children.description: A hypophosphite bath plates nickel onto the parts without an external current, by catalytic reduction on the brass surface. Because the deposit is amorphous nickel containing a few per cent of phosphorus, it is harder and more corrosion-resistant than pure electrolytic nickel and it does not need to be masked. It became the standard underplate for the whole connector industry by the mid-1980s.

facts.label: Era note
facts.value: electrolytic nickel was still the volume process in 1982; electroless took over later in the decade

children.name: Phosphorus from phosphate rock
children.description: The hypophosphite reducing agent is made from white phosphorus, which was still produced in the 1980s by the electric-furnace reduction of phosphate rock - a route that consumed very large tonnages of low-grade apatite for a few tens of kilograms of elemental phosphorus.
children.note: Electrothermal phosphorus production was still standard in 1982; the modern blast-furnace acid-route came in later.

facts.label: Route
facts.value: phosphate rock -> electric furnace -> P4 -> hypophosphite

children.name: Gold for the contact flash
children.description: Gold is deposited from a cyanide or sulphite bath, by immersion displacement onto the nickel or by electroplating with a gold strike. It is the one precious metal on an entire C64's connector set, applied as a sub-micron skin over several square centimetres - a deliberate economics of just enough gold to make the contact.

facts.label: Thickness used
facts.value: 0.03-0.5 um (a fraction of a microinch-to-half-microinch flash)

facts.label: Baths
facts.value: gold cyanide, gold sulphite, or immersion displacement

children.note: The cyanide gold baths of the period required strict effluent control and were the usual cause of plating-industry water pollution enforcement actions in the late 1970s and 1980s.

children.name: Gold cyanide plating bath
children.description: Gold is plated from an alkaline cyanide bath with a gold anode that dissolves to replenish the bath. The bath is deliberately kept extremely low in free cyanide and gold so that the gold itself is plated preferentially rather than the underlying base metal.

children.name: Sodium cyanide from salt
children.description: The plating bath chemistry, and the reason the cyanide gold plating shops needed strict effluent control and why the industry carried a persistent safety and pollution burden through the period.

children.name: Immersion gold flash
children.description: A displacement process: the nickel surface is briefly attacked by a cyanide solution and gold plates itself out by substitution, in a few tenths of a micron, with no current. It is fast, cheap and exactly the right thickness for a connector flash.

children.name: Doré bullion as the metal feed
children.description: Most industrial gold plating in 1982 was fed from dore bullion - a semi-pure gold-silver alloy - refined to the fine gold the plating shops bought. The dore itself was mostly refinery production from anode slimes and mined doré bullion, so the plating gold is not a separate supply chain from jewellery gold.

children.name: The silver in dore
children.description: Dore bars are mostly gold but carry 10-30 % silver, because silver is far cheaper to recover alongside gold than on its own account. That silver in turn came largely from lead-zinc and copper concentrates.

children.name: Connector housing: injection-moulded thermoplastic or phenolic
children.description: The insulator every connector sits in. Card-edge and card-guide style connectors used black glass-filled polyester or phenolic because it machines cleanly, has almost no moulding flow and stands soldering temperatures; D-sub and DIN shells used glass-filled nylon or PBT. All were injection-moulded in multi-cavity tools.

facts.label: Phenolic
facts.value: black glass-filled polyester (e.g. glass-fibre reinforced phenolic), UL94 V-0

facts.label: Thermoplastics
facts.value: PBT UL94 V-0, PA66 + 30-50 % glass, or LCP

children.note: The 24-pin user-port replacement connectors on sale today are specified as PBT UL94 V-0 insulator with gold-over-nickel contacts, which is a reasonable period-accurate call as a substitute for whatever Commodore's original supplier used.

children.name: Glass-filled phenolic (thermoset)
children.description: Phenol-formaldehyde resin reinforced with chopped glass fibre and moulded under heat and pressure. Extremely dimensionally stable, heat resistant and flame retardant, which is why black glass-filled phenolic is the classic black body of terminal blocks, card-edge sockets and relay bases. The disadvantage is that it cannot be melted and reformed, so every detail - including the card guide slot - has to be in the tool.

children.name: Chopped E-glass fibre
children.description: The reinforcement in a glass-filled phenolic or PBT housing. E-glass is a drawn alkali-free borosilicate, and the fibre is chopped to ~3-15 mm, sized with a coupling agent and blended into the resin just before the tool closes.
children.note: The silica chain is expanded in the board file; this node exists because the connector housing is where the glass actually shows up as a part.

children.name: Silica sand for the glass fibre
children.description: The glass fibre in a connector body begins as silica sand melted with limestone and dolomite. The same sand is used for window glass, and it is the same quartz that the crystal reactors grow from.

children.name: Phenolic compression press
children.description: A heated platen press with matched metal dies, pressing the thermoset compound to shape and curing it in the same operation. Compression rather than injection is what makes phenolic bodies cheap: the flow is short and the die is simple.

children.name: Phenol and formaldehyde
children.description: Phenol comes from cumene or chlorobenzene, both benzene derivatives; formaldehyde from methanol oxidation. So a black phenolic connector body is, like everything else on this board, two or three steps downstream of a steam cracker.

children.name: Phenol from cumene
children.description: Phenol was made almost entirely by the cumene process: cumene oxidised to cumene hydroperoxide, then acid-split to phenol and acetone. Both products of that split fed the phenolic and the epoxy chains.

children.name: Benzene from a steam cracker
children.description: Aromatic hydrocarbon recovered from the aromatics complex of a large cracker or from catalytic reforming of naphtha. The root of styrene, phenol, cumene, aniline and bisphenol.

children.name: PBT thermoplastic housing
children.description: Polybutylene terephthalate is moulded at normal injection temperatures, so a connector body can carry snap-fit features, pivot pins and cable strain-relief arms that a thermoset cannot. Glass-filled PBT was the standard D-sub and DIN shell material of the era, chosen for stiffness and low creep.
children.note: PBT was the dominant D-sub shell material through the 1980s; LCP (liquid crystal polymer) took over on premium parts later in the decade.

children.name: Dimethyl terephthalate and butanediol
children.description: PBT is a condensation polymer of DMT and 1,4-butanediol. DMT comes from paraxylene; butanediol came in the 1980s largely from maleic anhydride hydrogenation (a coal/route) or from butanediol dehydrogenation. Both are petrochemical or coal-chemical intermediates.

children.name: Paraxylene and DMT
children.description: Paraxylene is oxidised to terephthalic acid, esterified with methanol to DMT, then condensed with butanediol. Methanol was itself a cheap synthesis-gas product of that period, so DMT carries coal and gas chemistry as well as oil.

children.name: Naphtha
children.description: The light distillate between gasoline and kerosene, and the standard cracker feed. A refinery fraction of crude, not a geological product.

children.name: UV stabiliser and glass filler
children.description: PBT needs an ultraviolet absorber because it yellows and embrittles in light, plus a glass filler for stiffness. The absorber is a benzotriazole, and both additives are minor mass but were cost-relevant in a moulded part sold in tens of millions.

children.name: Injection moulding press and tool
children.description: A multi-cavity tool clamped between the platens of a screw injection moulder. The housing is a commodity: the same part is made in hundreds of thousands for the entire electronics industry, which is why connector housings cost less than the contacts inside them.

facts.label: Tool steel
facts.value: P20 or H13, hardened to ~48-52 HRC

children.note: The plastics and moulding chain is expanded in the plastics file.

children.name: Injection screw and barrel
children.description: A nitrided steel screw and barrel, heated to 230-280 C, plastifying the polymer and injecting it into the tool. The screw is itself a wear part made from tool steel, so the moulding industry is a steady consumer of alloy steel.

children.name: Mould tool steel
children.description: P20 stainless tool steel was the industry standard cavity steel in 1982, hardened to ~48-52 HRC and polished to a fine finish. A connector housing's surface is entirely a function of the cavity polish.

children.name: Iron ore behind P20 tool steel
children.description: AISI P20 is a low-alloy tool steel: iron with about half a per cent of chromium and a similar amount of molybdenum, made in the same alloy-steel shops as every other industrial tool.

children.name: User port, 24-pin card edge
children.description: The C64's expansion bus. A 24-position double-row card-edge socket, 3.96 mm pitch, carrying the address, data and control lines plus regulated and unregulated power out to user-port peripherals. Spare parts for this connector are specified as gold-over-nickel contacts in a PBT UL94 V-0 insulator, which is a fair description of the period part.

facts.label: Contacts
facts.value: gold over nickel, in PBT UL94 V-0

facts.label: Carries
facts.value: 12 data/address lines, /RESET, /CASS lines, +5 V, 9 V AC, GND

children.name: Gold-over-nickel card-edge contacts
children.description: Each contact is a formed spring leaf whose nose protrudes from the insulator and sweeps the mating card's copper edge as it slides in. The wiping action means the gold never has to be thick to stay clean, and the nickel beneath carries the solder joint to the board.

children.name: Spring leaf alloy
children.description: The leaf has to both wipe the mating edge and hold a contact force, so it is a hard-worked copper alloy - phosphor bronze or a brass-tempered strip. It is the same material family as the switch contacts and the cartridge socket.

children.name: Copper ore for the leaf
children.description: Chalcopyrite and native copper, refined to cathode and rolled. The contact-leaf and switch-leaf trades drew on the same copper rod as the winding wire and the board traces.

children.name: Solder tail and wave-solder attachment
children.description: The tail is formed flat and pierced so it takes a fillet in the wave-solder bath, giving a mechanically strong joint that also resists the repeated flexing of a plugged-in peripheral cable.

children.name: Through-hole tail and wave joint
children.description: A pierced rectangular tail that takes a large fillet in the wave bath. The joint has to survive a peripheral cable being pulled.

children.name: User-port pin functions
children.description: Pins 1-12 carry +5 V out, ground, /RESET, /PPASS (the CPU-select line), the cassette sense/write/read lines and the cassette motor line, plus 9 V AC; pins 13-24 carry the user port's serial bus lines (/EOT, /SERCLK, /ATN IN, /ATN OUT) and the speaker and cassette-slot lines. The C64 6510's on-chip I/O port is wired straight into this connector, which is why a printer interface or a modem could hang directly off it.
children.note: The broad grouping of signals is well documented; I have not verified every individual pin number for this connector and the C64's documentation is inconsistent between the breadbin and the C64C.

children.name: Cassette (datasette) port, 2 x 6 card edge
children.description: The port that reads and writes Commodore DATAsette tapes. It is a 12-position card-edge socket - six contacts on each face, 3.96 mm pitch - that mates with a 6-pin connector on the datasette lead. Carrying analogue audio, motor control and a sense line, it is a reminder that in 1982 'I/O' still meant tape.

facts.label: Signals
facts.value: ground, 5 V, motor control, serial read, serial write, sense

children.name: Cassette read pull-up resistor
children.description: The /FLAG input of CIA #1 that senses a keypress is pulled up through a 3.3 kOhm resistor, part of the resistor array family described under mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks. It is a tiny detail that shows the whole board's design logic: discrete resistors where few are needed, a printed array where many identical ones are.
children.note: The pull-up is more properly documented as a discrete 3.3 kOhm resistor than as part of RP3/RP4; I have linked the concept, not the part number.

children.name: The 3k3 pull-up as a discrete part
children.description: The datasette sense/flag line is held high by a single 3.3 kOhm 1/4 W resistor on the board. It is one of the values shared with the bussed resistor arrays, which is a good illustration of how the board mixes array and discrete for the same resistance.

children.name: Same carbon film supply chain
children.description: The 3k3 is one of the ordinary carbon film resistors whose chain is described at mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.carbon-film.

children.name: Why the port exists at all
children.description: The port carries analogue audio plus three DC control lines. The C64 read FSK-encoded data by timing transitions on the read line and generating the tones on the write line - the whole tape interface is three transistors, a resistor and two electrolytics, which is why it is so sensitive to capacitor leakage.

children.name: Cartridge / expansion port, 44-pin dual card edge
children.description: The slot along the bottom of the case into which cartridges plug. A 44-position dual female card-edge socket in a black glass-filled polyester body, with phosphor-bronze contacts gold-flashed over nickel. It is the single most-scrutinised connector on the machine: its contacts carry the entire address and data bus and have to survive thousands of cartridge insertions.

facts.label: Gender
facts.value: female socket; the cartridge has the male edge

children.name: Moulded card guide and polarising key
children.description: The socket body doubles as the mechanical guide: a moulded channel sets the card's insertion depth, and an asymmetric keyway stops a cartridge being inserted the wrong way round. Because the body is a thermoset, the guide is machined or moulded in one piece and cannot flex.
children.note: The C64 cartridge connector's guide and keyway are visible in photographs of the underside of the board; I have not measured the keyway dimensions.

children.name: Machined guide features
children.description: Because the socket body is a thermoset, the card channel, the stop face and the polarising key cannot be melted into place - they have to be present in the compression tool or machined afterwards. Both were normal for this part in 1982.

children.name: Glass fibre of the filled phenolic
children.description: Chopped glass fibre in the phenolic is what stops the guide wearing when a cartridge is pushed and pulled thousands of times. It is the same filler as in the connector housings.

children.name: Contact alignment and pitch
children.description: At 2.54 mm pitch across 44 positions, the accumulation of tolerance is what makes or breaks a card-edge socket: the tool and the plating process have to hold the contacts on a common plane so no single contact is left proud and taking all the wear.

children.name: Contact wear and the 'dead cartridge' problem
children.description: A card-edge socket is a wear item: each insertion plucks the leaf contacts and sweeps the mating gold edge. Dust, oxide from the cartridge's board and accumulated plasticiser eventually make one or two contacts intermittent, which is the classic 'dead cartridge' symptom. Contact cleaning and, on a well-used machine, contact replacement were the routine repair.

children.name: Contact cleaning regime
children.description: The routine service answer to a marginal cartridge socket: an alcohol swab on the contacts, a foam rod through the slots, and a bend of the leaf if it has lost tension. It is one of the few repairs on a 1982 machine that needs no parts.

children.name: Commodore expansion port specification
children.description: The 44-pin socket's pin assignment, pitch and card thickness were Commodore's own definition rather than a JEDEC standard, which is why cartridges for the C64, C128 and VIC-20 are interchangeable and C64C cartridges are not.

children.name: Phosphor bronze contacts
children.description: Phosphor bronze was the standard card-edge contact alloy for this connector, gold-flashed over nickel. It is springy, fatigue-resistant and takes a good plating - the combination a card-edge socket needs, because it is wiped hard on every insertion.

children.name: Tin in the bronze
children.description: The tin that makes the contact alloy springy came from cassiterite, mined and smelted.

children.name: Cassiterite workings
children.description: Heavy, chemically inert tin oxide that concentrates in placers below pegmatites and in alluvial gravels. Because it is so dense it also turns up in gold placer concentrates, where it was historically an impurity to be discarded.

children.name: Selective gold plating of the contact area
children.description: The contact is selectively plated by tabbing: the terminal is masked or wired as a cathode so only the mating area is gold-flashed.

children.name: Video/audio connector, 8-pin round DIN
children.description: One round DIN on the rear panel carrying composite video, separate luma and chroma (for a Commodore 1701 monitor's RGB-with-separate-luma input), mono audio, and the RF modulator's composite and audio out. Very early 1982 boards used a 5-pin version instead, with luma and chroma combined.

facts.label: Mounting
facts.value: screwed to the case and soldered to the board

children.name: Sprung split-tulip centre pin
children.description: The centre contact is a thin slotted pin that is sprung into a slight taper, so it plugs into a matching conical socket and self-aligns. The slot lets it flex elastically and also means a slightly undersized mating hole still makes contact at two lines rather than at a point - which is why DIN connectors are famously forgiving.

facts.label: Engagement force
facts.value: low, thanks to the tapered split

children.name: Conical mating socket
children.description: The socket the tulip pin plugs into has a matching taper, usually machined or stamped with a broach, so the two surfaces self-align on insertion. The taper is the reason a DIN plug feels forgiving and a plain pin-and-socket does not.

children.name: Broached taper
children.description: The mating socket's cone is broached rather than turned, so the surface finish is controlled by a single multi-form tool. The broach was hardened steel, so this was another tool-steel consumer.

children.name: Iron ore
children.description: Hematite and magnetite, the iron ore of the world trade. Everything ferrous in this file - springs, shafts, stamping dies, tool steel, cast-iron kiln parts - begins here.

children.name: Contact plating of the DIN pin
children.description: The centre pin is nickel-plated with a gold or silver flash; the signal level here (composite video and line-level audio) is high enough that nickel alone would work, but gold was used for consistency with the other connectors.

children.name: Nickel underplate plus precious flash
children.description: The same nickel-then-gold sequence as every other contact in the machine, on a tin or nickel base.

children.name: Nickel-plated steel shell and shield can
children.description: The outer barrel is a drawn steel shell, nickel-plated for corrosion resistance and solderability, and crimped around the insulator. On a metal-panel or rear-case mounting it doubles as the shell ground. Nickel plate on steel is the standard 1982 finish for a mains-adjacent chassis connector.

children.name: Drawn steel shell stock
children.description: The barrel is deep-drawn from nickel-plated steel strip - a two-and-a-half type can be drawn in a few progressive strokes. The nickel plate carries the shell ground and resists the corrosion a rear-panel connector sees.

children.name: Iron ore to strip steel
children.description: Hot-rolled strip from a continuous caster, cold-rolled and annealed. The strip trade is downstream of the same ore-to-pig-iron chain as everything else ferrous.

children.name: Shell knurl and bayonet ring
children.description: The knurled ring on a DIN plug is what a user grips to unscrew it; on a socket the threaded barrel screws into the panel. The knurl is rolled into the shell in the same draw.

children.name: Knurl rolling
children.description: The knurl is rolled into the shell in the drawing die by a knurled wheel, because knurling a drawn can after plating would cut through the nickel.

children.name: Serial bus connector, 6-pin round DIN
children.description: The IEC serial bus that daisy-chained the 1541 disk drive, printers and the rest of Commodore's peripheral family. Same body and same stamping technology as the video connector, smaller pin count, and the same sprung centre pin.

facts.label: Carries
facts.value: serial data in/out, clock in/out, atn in/out, ground, +5 V

children.name: IEEE-488-style handshake on 6 wires
children.description: Commodore's bus ran clock and data in both directions with attention lines and handshaking on every transfer - an IEEE-488 descendant. That is why a C64 could sit between two 1541 drives and still address the right one: the addressing is on the bus, not in the drive.
children.note: Commodore's serial bus is an IEEE-488-influenced protocol but not literally IEEE-488; the source reference is indicative. The bus pin count and function split are well documented.

children.name: Control ports, 2 x DE-9 subminiature D
children.description: The two nine-pin D-sub sockets on the rear panel for joystick or paddle controllers, a light pen or a mouse. Each is a DE-9 female in a plastic D-shaped shell with gold-flashed brass contacts dimpled for reliable mating - the connector everyone remembers from Atari, Commodore and Amiga alike.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: DE-9, female, right angle, plastic shell

facts.label: Contacts
facts.value: stamped brass, gold-flashed over nickel, dimpled

facts.label: Shell
facts.value: glass-filled nylon or PBT with a nickel-plated metal shroud on some types

children.name: Dimpled contact and shell-ground design
children.description: Each female contact carries a dimple on its mating face. Dimpling pushes the two contact surfaces into a defined line contact rather than a random point contact, which lowers the contact resistance and stops the surfaces rolling on each other. The plug's outer shell also contacts the socket shroud, so the plug's ground comes from its metal shell rather than from its pins.

facts.label: Contact plating
facts.value: 30 microinch gold over nickel, standard for the era

children.name: D-subminiature (MIL-DTL-24308) standard
children.description: The D-sub was standardised for military/aerospace use in the 1950s and became universal electronics furniture. Its 2.77 mm pitch, D-shaped polarised shell and 2.5 mm panel-mount screw pattern are defined by the standard; the C64's control ports are ordinary commercial DE-9 sockets.

children.name: DE-9 insulator
children.description: A black glass-filled thermoplastic insulator carrying the nine contacts, keyed to the metal shell. It has to hold position to a few hundredths of a millimetre because the contacts must all engage simultaneously in a stiff nine-pin plug.

children.name: Glass-filled nylon insulator
children.description: Glass-filled PA66 holds nine contact positions to a few hundredths of a millimetre over a plastic D-shell, and it takes the insertion force of a stiff nine-pin plug without cracking.

children.name: Caprolactam
children.description: Nylon-6-6 from caprolactam, itself from benzene-derived cyclohexanone. The same chain as the switch body and the keycap.

children.name: Benzene from a steam cracker
children.description: Aromatic hydrocarbon recovered from the aromatics complex of a large cracker or from catalytic reforming of naphtha. The root of styrene, phenol, cumene, aniline and bisphenol.

children.name: Metal shell shroud and strain relief
children.description: On the machine side the socket is a plastic-shell type with no metal shroud; the shroud is on the cable plug, where it is what provides the plug's shell ground and its mechanical strength. Both were stamped and plated the same way.

children.name: Shroud stamping and plating
children.description: The cable plug's metal shroud is stamped from brass strip and nickel-plated; it provides the plug's shell ground and its mechanical strength, and it is what the user grips.

children.name: Power inlet, 7-pin round DIN
children.description: The rear-panel socket the external PSU brick plugs into. A 7-pin round connector in a large 'type C' shell, following the DIN 45329 / IEC 10 form: pins 1 and 5 carry the regulated +5 V DC and pins 6 and 7 the 9 V AC from the transformer, with the switched side feeding the board through L5, C97, C100 and SW1.
children.note: CORRECTION to the brief: the C64 power connector is 7-pin, not 6. Sources agree on 7 pins; some 1982 supplies shipped a lead with only four populated contacts, which is a different and well-documented issue (the 'pin 5 damage' fault).

facts.label: Standard
facts.value: DIN 45329 / IEC 10 style, large type C shell

facts.label: Pin 1 and 5
facts.value: +5 V DC from the regulator, filtered by L5, C97 and C100

children.name: Friction-lock and pull-proof contacts
