children.description: A mains-adjacent DC supply connector needs its contacts to survive being tugged by the cable. The mating pins are a friction type with a deliberately stiff crimp barrel so a pull is taken by the metal, not the solder fillet; some Commodore supplies additionally used a friction-lock retention ring on the plug body.
children.note: The brief's 'friction-lock contacts' description matches the pull-proof crimp on this connector; I have not found a C64-specific retention-ring part number.

children.name: Crimp barrel construction
children.description: The pin is a hollow brass tube with an interference crimp onto the conductor rather than a solder joint. That is the actual meaning of a friction-lock contact: the metal grips the metal, so a tug on the cable is carried by a mechanical interference fit and not by the solder fillet.

children.name: Brass pin stock
children.description: Cartridge brass drawn wire, the standard material for crimp contacts because it is springy enough to hold an interference fit yet soft enough to take the crimp without cracking.

children.name: Copper ore to brass
children.description: Brass is a copper-zinc alloy, so it begins at a copper ore and a zinc ore. Both are ancient mined materials and both were still being mined rather than synthesised in 1982.

children.name: The pin 5 damage fault
children.description: One of the best-known Commodore power faults: a partially populated or incorrectly wired supply lead damages the 5 V pin in the machine's socket, so the machine will not power up even with a known-good supply. It is a wear-and-misalignment problem on a friction contact carrying a DC load that the connector was not designed to be unplugged under.
children.note: Widely reported in Commodore service literature; I have not verified a primary factory bulletin on it.

children.name: SW1 switching of the 5 V rail
children.description: The socket feeds straight into the board's main filter (L5, C97, C100) and then through switch SW1, so SW1 breaks the load current rather than the supply - which is why the switch's contact rating looks absurdly high for the job. The external brick's own rocker does the real mains isolation; SW1 only breaks DC at a few amps.
children.note: The L5/C97/C100/SW1 ordering is from Commodore's own service manual text on the power supply.

children.name: Keyboard ribbon header
children.description: A soldered pin header at the front-left edge of the mainboard carrying the keyboard's flat ribbon cable. The keyboard's matrix lines and the shift-lock return run out of the machine this way; it is the one connector on the board that is not an industry-standard part but a plain 2.54 mm row of pins.
children.note: I could not establish the exact position count of the C64 keyboard header from a primary source. C64 repair references consistently describe a 2.54 mm-pitch male header along the front-left board edge, and replacement parts are sold as 2.54 mm rows of varying length; I have therefore described it generically rather than committing to a pin count. The matrix needs at most 8 column lines plus 8 row lines plus shift-lock and the 6510 I/O port lines, so a 2 x 12 (24-way) header is plausible but unverified.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: soldered straight male header on the PCB

children.name: Wave-soldered pin header
children.description: The header's pins were pushed into the board and wave-soldered in one pass with the rest of the components, in 63/37 lead-tin solder. That is why the pin material is brass with a tin plate rather than nickel: it wets tin-lead, and it does not need the corrosion resistance a gold-plated control-port contact does.
children.note: The leaded-solder claim matches the era; the interconnect file carries the solder chemistry.

children.name: 63/37 lead-tin solder
children.description: The alloy that joined every part on the board. Snelled with a small amount of lead to make it flow better at a low temperature, it has a eutectic at 183 C. The lead came from galena, the ore of lead, and the tin from cassiterite - two of the oldest traded metals, both still mined rather than synthesised in 1982.
children.note: Commodore did not use lead-free solder on the breadbin mainboard; the lead-free transition in consumer electronics did not begin until the 1990s and was driven by RoHS in 2006.

children.name: Galena (lead ore)
children.description: Lead came from galena, PbS, a dense cubic mineral mined underground often as a by-product of silver and zinc. It is roasted and sintered to litharge and reduced in a blast furnace - the same cupellation metallurgy that has produced lead for three thousand years.

children.name: Flux and its origin
children.description: Rosin flux, dissolved in alcohol, cleaned the board in the wave-solder bath. Rosin is the sticky residue of pine trees, and the cleaning step after soldering removes it because ionic residue is what makes a board drift or corrode.

children.name: Pine rosin
children.description: Rosin is the fossilised sticky resin of conifers, dissolved in alcohol as the soldering flux and then washed off because ionic residue causes drift and corrosion.

children.name: Softwood resin
children.description: Collected from pine and conifer stands; the tree that keeps the board clean.

children.name: Wave-soldering machine
children.description: A pumped solder pot with a travelling wave, a heated conveyor and pre- and post-heating tunnels. The whole C64 board went through one wave in about ten seconds; that is why the pins were tinned and the leads formed for a flat joint.

roots.name: Keyboard matrix switches and domes
roots.description: How one keystroke on a C64 becomes a 1 in memory: 63 rubber domes on a rigid printed circuit board, scanned by CIA #1 as an 8 x 8 matrix. The domes are carbon-loaded rubber pills that short two plated pads when a keycap's plunger drives them closed, and the scanned result is simply a pair of row and column lines being connected.
roots.note: CORRECTION to the brief in one respect: the C64 keyboard is NOT a flexible membrane with silver-ink traces. It is a rubber-dome keyboard on a RIGID printed circuit board with plated conductive pads, and the domes themselves are the conductive element. Earlier VIC-20-generation Commodore keyboards also used rigid boards with bare (unplated) copper pads, which oxidise - the reason some early C64 keyboards need cleaning while later ones do not. Commodore did use silver-filled ink pads on some other keyboards and peripherals of the period, so that branch is included, but it is not the breadbin C64.

facts.label: Keys
facts.value: 63 (including 5 cursor keys); matrix directly covers 64 of 66 positions

facts.label: Matrix
facts.value: 8 columns driven on CIA #1 port A, 8 rows read on port B

facts.label: Domed keys
facts.value: 61 of the 63; SHIFT LOCK is wired on the same line as LSHIFT

facts.label: Out-of-matrix
facts.value: RESTORE (wired to NMI) and SHIFT LOCK

children.name: 8 x 8 keyboard matrix
children.description: Eight column lines snake around the board and eight row lines snake around the other way, each pair of crossing traces forming one key. Pressing a key connects its column to its row; the firmware walks the matrix by writing a pattern to CIA #1's port A and reading port B. Because one row line can touch eight different columns, a single conducting bridge is the entire 'switch'.

facts.label: Scan
facts.value: write column pattern to $DC00, read rows from $DC01

facts.label: Latency
facts.value: one scan per ~1/60 s frame unless idle

facts.label: Ghosting
facts.value: 3-key combinations can produce an extra false key - the classic matrix ghosting problem

children.name: Rigid keyboard PCB with plated pads
children.description: A glass-epoxy laminate board, drilled and plated through in the usual way, carrying the matrix traces as copper and terminating each key position in a pair of plated pads. On the breadbin keyboard the pads are plated metal; on the earlier VIC-20-derived boards they were bare copper, and bare copper oxidises into a high-resistance film - the reason those keyboards need periodic cleaning and later ones generally do not.

facts.label: Construction
facts.value: rigid FR-4, not a flex membrane

facts.label: Pads
facts.value: plated through-hole pads on breadbin boards; bare copper on earliest

facts.label: Mounting
facts.value: standoffs and screws into the case, not clips

children.note: The bare-copper-pad claim comes from a restoration account of an early (VIC-20-derived) C64 keyboard which notes its activation pads are not protected from oxidation the way later keyboards' are. The PCB materials and fabrication are expanded in the board file.

children.name: Electrodeposited copper foil
children.description: The matrix traces are copper, deposited on the laminate by an electroplating line using acid copper sulphate solution and an insoluble anode. The same copper foil process as the mainboard, at a much thinner gauge.

children.name: Chalcopyrite (CuFeS2)
children.description: The dominant copper ore, mined underground in porphyry and skarn deposits and in open pits. Copper was electrorefined to cathode and rolled into foil long before it was ever plated onto a board; the board industry simply bought the foil that the copper industry already made.

children.name: Plating of the key pads
children.description: The exposed pads are plated - gold over nickel on later keyboards - so the carbon contact of the rubber dome has a low-resistance, non-oxidising surface to bridge onto. Where the plating is absent or has worn through, the bare copper oxidises and the key needs cleaning.

children.name: Gold for the pad flash
children.description: A thin gold flash over nickel on the key pads. Gold does not oxidise, so the dome keeps making contact for decades; where the flash is thin or gone, the key stops working until cleaned.

children.name: Glass-epoxy laminate (FR-4)
children.description: Woven glass-fibre cloth impregnated with epoxy and pressed into a sheet. The standard printed-circuit laminate since the 1960s, replacing the older phenolic paper board. The keyboard board is a trivial two-layer FR-4 part, but it goes through the same copper foil lamination and hole-drilling lines as a mainboard.
children.note: The glass fabric is drawn from molten glass (silica); the chemistry chain is expanded in the board file.

children.name: Woven E-glass cloth
children.description: Silica glass is melted and drawn into fine filaments a few microns across, woven into a cloth and woven again into a fine gauze. This cloth is the reinforcement in every FR-4 board in the world.

children.name: Silica batch from silica sand
children.description: The glass batch is made from silica sand with limestone and dolomite as fluxes. The sand is dredged or quarried, and it is the same quartz sand that fed the hydrothermal quartz reactors.
children.note: The quartz sand node is shared with mb.crystal; referenced rather than duplicated.

children.name: Glass batch formulation
children.description: Silica sand with limestone and dolomite as fluxes, and a little salt as a catalyst, melted at ~1400-1600 C. The same batch chemistry as container glass, only drawn rather than floated.

children.name: Epoxy resin of the laminate
children.description: The epoxy that binds the glass cloth is derived from bisphenol A and epichlorohydrin, both of which are petrochemical. A two-layer keyboard PCB is thus a woven silica sheet glued with a fossil-derived resin and clad in copper.

children.name: Epichlorohydrin
children.description: One of the two building blocks of epoxy resin, made by chlorinating propylene with hypochlorous acid. Epoxy is used on the keyboard laminate, on the capacitor bungs, on the tantalum seals and on the connector overmoulds - one of the most widespread materials on the whole machine.

children.name: Crude oil
children.description: The hydrocarbon root of every polymer, solvent, ink and flux on the machine. The refining chain from crude through steam cracking to monomers is expanded in the plastics and fluids files.

children.name: Carbon-loaded rubber domes
children.description: Each key position has a small moulded rubber pill, domed upwards, whose underside carries a conductive carbon-loaded contact that bridges two pads when the dome is crushed. Because carbon is loaded into the rubber as a filler rather than plated on, the dome is its own contact - it wears slightly with use and it is the consumable part of the switch.

facts.label: Fill
facts.value: carbon black or graphite powder in a silicone or neoprene elastomer

facts.label: Activation force
facts.value: ~150-250 g on the dome alone, plus the keycap spring

facts.label: Life
facts.value: ~millions of actuations, but the conductive face tarnishes with skin oil and dust

children.name: Carbon-filled elastomer compound
children.description: Carbon black is compounded into the elastomer at a few tens of per cent by weight. The particles form a percolation network so the dome conducts along its own bulk, and the higher the loading the lower the resistance - but too much loading makes the dome brittle. This is the same black powder that goes into resistor films and pot tracks.

facts.label: Contact resistance
facts.value: typically tens to hundreds of ohms - enough to trip a CMOS input, far too much for a logic 'low'

children.note: The dome resistance being in the tens-to-hundreds of ohms range is why a dirty dome still 'works' for a 6526 input but why cleaning it matters; the characteristic failure is drift upward into the CMOS threshold region.

children.name: Silicone or neoprene elastomer
children.description: The dome body. Silicone (polydimethylsiloxane) was favoured for its high compression set and wide temperature range; neoprene (polychloroprene) for oil and abrasion resistance. Both are thermoset elastomers, vulcanised in the mould rather than injection-moulded as thermoplastics, which is why they are compression-moulded sheet.
children.note: Which elastomer the C64's dome sheet used is not something I could determine; both were standard.

children.name: Silicone dome compound
children.description: Silicone rubber is built on a silicon-oxygen backbone and is filled with reinforcing silica. It stays elastic over a wide temperature range and does not take up much oil, which is why a silicone dome does not swell and seize.

children.name: Silica sand
children.description: Quartz sand, the feedstock for glass, for frits and glazes, and for the hydrothermal growth of synthetic quartz. Dredged from beaches or quarried from ancient dune deposits.

children.name: Carbon black filler (petroleum-derived)
children.description: The same furnace-black feedstock used in the resistors, compounded into the elastomer. The dome's conductivity and its wear rate are both set by the grade and loading of this powder.
children.note: The full carbon-black tree is at mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.carbon-film.powder.carbon-black; referenced rather than duplicated.

children.name: Grade selection for the dome
children.description: A high-structure furnace black gives a stronger percolation network at lower loading, so a dome can be made conductive with less filler and stay soft. The grade choice is the difference between a responsive key and a stiff one.

children.name: Compression moulding of the dome sheet
children.description: The domes are moulded as a continuous sheet on a heated platen press: uncured compound is placed in a multi-cavity tool, pressed, cured, and the sheet released as one piece with every key's dome attached. Domes therefore arrive as a single printed-circuit-sized rubber sheet that has to be aligned to the pads by hand.

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: ~150-180 C, minutes, for silicone; ~100-140 C for neoprene

children.note: Compression-moulded dome sheets were standard; whether the C64's came as a sheet or pre-applied to a carrier film I could not determine.

children.name: Heated platen press
children.description: A hydraulic flat-bed press with heated platens holds a multi-cavity dome tool against the compound long enough to cure the elastomer. Small presses of this type did the whole dome sheet for a keyboard in one shot.

children.name: Steel dome tool
children.description: A machined or spark-eroded steel tool with one hemispherical cavity per key. It has to be replaced as the dome geometry is re-specified, and its surface finish is what the dome's mating face is polished against.

children.name: Spark-erosion machining of the dome cavity
children.description: A fine copper electrode is brought within micrometres of the workpiece in a dielectric bath and pulses of a few microseconds melt a microscopic crater per pulse. Spark erosion is how a one-micron hemispherical cavity gets cut in hardened tool steel without any mechanical stress on the surface.

children.name: Graphite tool electrode
children.description: Graphite is the standard spark-erosion electrode: it is conductive, machinable to a fine tip, and wears slowly by re-graphitising. Machined graphite is made from petroleum coke calcined at ~3000 C.

children.name: Keycap and plunger mechanism
children.description: A double-shot moulded keycap on a cross-shaped plastic stem. The stem sits in a plunger barrel and carries either a coil spring back up (the common later C64 keycap) or, on the earliest VIC-20-derived keyboards, nothing at all - those rely purely on the rubber dome for their return and feel markedly sluggish.

facts.label: Construction
facts.value: double-shot moulded ABS or ABS/PC, legend printed or moulded

facts.label: Plunger
facts.value: moulded plastic cross stem in a barrel

facts.label: Return
facts.value: coil spring in later keycaps; absent on the earliest keyboards

children.name: ABS keycap polymer
children.description: Acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene: a styrene-acrylonitrile matrix rubberised with polybutadiene. It is tough, dimensionally stable, chemically scratch-resistant and - crucially for legends - it takes paint and plating well. Almost every C64 keycap is ABS or ABS/PC.

facts.label: Why ABS
facts.value: impact strength plus the ability to hold a printed legend

children.name: Polybutadiene rubber phase
children.description: The elastic phase that makes ABS impact-resistant, made by polymerising butadiene derived from refinery butadiene, which itself comes from steam cracking propylene. This is the hydrocarbon tree: propylene to butadiene to the rubber in the keycap's grip surface.
children.note: The steam-cracking-to-polymer chain is expanded in the plastics file.

children.name: Butadiene monomer
children.description: The rubber phase of ABS is made from butadiene, produced by steam cracking of refinery butane or by dehydrogenating butenes. It is the same butadiene the synthetic-rubber industry used.

children.name: Crude oil
children.description: The hydrocarbon root of every polymer, solvent, ink and flux on the machine. The refining chain from crude through steam cracking to monomers is expanded in the plastics and fluids files.

children.name: Styrene monomer
children.description: Produced by dehydrogenating ethylbenzene, itself made by alkylating benzene with ethylene from steam cracking. Styrene is the rigid phase of the copolymer; benzene is ultimately a refinery product of crude oil or of pyrolitic gasoline from steam crackers.
children.note: Chain expanded in the plastics file.

children.name: Ethylbenzene to styrene
children.description: Benzene is alkylated with ethylene to ethylbenzene, then dehydrogenated to styrene over a promoted iron oxide catalyst.

children.name: Naphtha
children.description: The light distillate between gasoline and kerosene, and the standard cracker feed. A refinery fraction of crude, not a geological product.

children.name: Acrylonitrile monomer
children.description: The acrylonitrile monomer is made by the Sohlo process: propylene, ammonia and oxygen are passed over a bismuth-antimony or bismuth-molybdenum catalyst to give acrylonitrile selectively. Propylene itself comes from steam cracking of naphtha, so the keycap of a C64 is roughly one and a half hydrocarbon molecules away from crude oil.

children.name: Bismuth-antimony catalyst
children.description: The ammoxidation catalyst is a bismuth molybdate or bismuth-antimony promoted silica. Bismuth came from bismuthinite, a comparatively rare ore worked chiefly in Bolivia and China, and it was a real bottleneck for acrylonitrile capacity in the 1980s.
children.note: Bismuth supply was genuinely tight in the early 1980s and the ammoxidation catalyst industry was a significant consumer; flagged medium because I have not quantified it.

children.name: Double-shot moulding of the legend
children.description: The keycap is injection-moulded twice: once in the base colour, then a second shot of a second colour is injected into a slightly larger cavity, covering everything except the legend characters, which were left as uncoated islands of the first shot. This gives a legend that cannot wear off - the reason a forty-year-old C64 keycap still reads.

facts.label: Shots
facts.value: two injection mouldings, co-moulded in the same tool cycle

facts.label: Legend
facts.value: island of the base-colour shot, not a printed decal

children.note: Double-shot keycaps were standard on quality keyboards of the period; whether every C64 keycap of 1982 was double-shot rather than pad-printed varies by supplier and I have not verified it for the whole set.

children.name: Second-shot colour
children.description: The outer shot is pigmented with an organic or inorganic colourant at high loading. Brown, red, orange and grey legends - the four C64 keycap colours - are all achievable with pigmented ABS; the moulding must be run at a high enough pressure that the two shots fuse rather than delaminate.

children.name: Colourant in the second shot
children.description: The second-shot colour is a pigment dispersed in the ABS matrix at high loading. Organic pigments give brighter colours and are more expensive; inorganic iron oxides give the earthier browns and reds.

children.name: Iron oxide pigments
children.description: Synthetic iron oxides, made by oxidising iron scrap, were the standard browns, reds and blacks of the period and are still used. They begin at iron ore and end up in the keycap.

children.name: Iron ore
children.description: Hematite and magnetite, the iron ore of the world trade. Everything ferrous in this file - springs, shafts, stamping dies, tool steel, cast-iron kiln parts - begins here.

children.name: Co-moulding cycle
children.description: Both shots are moulded in one press cycle using a hot-runner or a runnerless hot manifold so the second colour is injected onto the first while the first is still hot enough to bond. That is what makes the legend wear-proof rather than a coat of paint.

children.name: Coil return spring
children.description: A small stainless or music-wire spring inside the plunger barrel returning the key to its rest position and setting the initial (pre-dome) force. Without it the user bottoms out on the dome itself, which is why the earliest keyboards feel hard and inconsistent.
children.note: Music wire (high-carbon steel) or stainless; the spring wire is wound on a small coil-winder in the millions.

children.name: Music wire (patented steel)
children.description: A high-carbon steel wire, patented and drawn to a fine diameter, with a very high tensile strength - which is what lets a millimetre-thick coil inside a keycap return thousands of times without taking a set.

children.name: Iron ore for spring steel
children.description: The same hematite/magnetite chain as the joystick shaft. Almost all ferrous stock in 1982 was basic-oxygen-furnace steel from imported ore.

children.name: Spring coiling machine
children.description: A cam-controlled coiler winds a coil spring from wire, sets its free length and closes the ends, tens of thousands per hour. Every keycap plunger spring on the keyboard was made on a machine of this type.

children.name: Tool steel cam and dies
children.description: The coiler tool is hardened tool steel, and the coiler is a Camweld or similar automatic machine. Ferrous tooling, so iron ore again.

children.name: Iron ore
children.description: Hematite and magnetite, the iron ore of the world trade. Everything ferrous in this file - springs, shafts, stamping dies, tool steel, cast-iron kiln parts - begins here.

children.name: SHIFT LOCK and RESTORE, the two off-matrix keys
children.description: Two of the 63 keys are not in the scanned matrix. SHIFT LOCK is wired to the same line as LSHIFT, so the firmware cannot distinguish it and simply sees a latched shift. RESTORE is wired directly to the 6510's NMI line, so pressing it halts the CPU without any firmware involvement at all - a hardware reset, not a key.

facts.label: SHIFT LOCK
facts.value: wired to the same wire as LSHIFT

facts.label: RESTORE
facts.value: wired to NMI, outside the matrix entirely

children.note: Documented on the C64 wiki keyboard page. SHIFT LOCK is a latching dome arrangement (the dome is deformed or a second contact is added) rather than a scanner-visible key.

children.name: Latching dome for SHIFT LOCK
children.description: A dome that latches: pressing it collapses it and it stays collapsed, requiring a second, firmer press (or a press on a neighbouring key) to release. Mechanically it is a deformation of the rubber dome itself rather than a separate switch, which is why no space in the matrix is spent on it.

children.name: Bistable dome geometry
children.description: The latching dome works because the rubber is shaped so that under a light press it collapses past the rubber's own elastic limit and stays collapsed. It is a mechanical latch, not an electrical one, which is why the firmware has no idea a separate key exists.

children.name: Wiring to the LSHIFT line
children.description: SHIFT LOCK is simply wired in parallel with LSHIFT, so the firmware cannot tell the two apart: pressing SHIFT LOCK just holds the shift bit down. Restore is on a completely different wire, straight to the 6510 NMI pin.

children.name: Flat ribbon cable to the mainboard
children.description: A flat multi-conductor ribbon leaves the keyboard board, loops through the case, and terminates at the pin header on the front-left edge of the mainboard. The ribbon is crimped into an insulation-displacement connector on the keyboard end in later designs, and soldered directly to the header on the mainboard end.

facts.label: Construction
facts.value: flat flexible cable, PVC-jacketed, 0.5-1.27 mm pitch

facts.label: Failure mode
facts.value: conductor fatigue fracture at the header - the single most common C64 keyboard fault

children.note: Fatigue fracture where the ribbon flexes at the header is by far the most-reported C64 keyboard fault of the period and later; it produces keys that work only when the cable is bent a certain way.

children.name: PET/PVC flat flexible cable
children.description: Parallel copper conductors laminated between polyester film layers with a PVC jacket. The jacket and the film are all hydrocarbon polymers, so this cable is chemically the same family as the switch housings and the case.
children.note: Insulation-displacement contacts on the keyboard end were common from the late 1970s; some Commodore designs used soldered connections at both ends.

children.name: PVC jacket
children.description: The ribbon's outer jacket is extruded PVC, the cheapest flexible insulation available. Vinyl chloride is made by oxychlorinating ethylene with chlorine, and the chlorine comes from salt - rock salt mined or solution-mined - while the ethylene comes from a steam cracker. So the ribbon cable ends at both rock salt and crude oil.
children.note: The salt-to-chlorine step is expanded in the fluids file.

children.name: Vinyl chloride monomer
children.description: Vinyl chloride is made by oxychlorinating ethylene with chlorine over a promoted catalyst. The ethylene comes from a steam cracker and the chlorine from brine electrolysis - so the ribbon jacket touches both an oil field and a salt field.

children.name: Naphtha
children.description: The light distillate between gasoline and kerosene, and the standard cracker feed. A refinery fraction of crude, not a geological product.

roots.name: Joystick controller
roots.description: The self-centring 4-way joystick Commodore bundled with the C64 and sold with most of its software: a moulded gate plate held neutral by four springs, four miniature microswitches underneath it, a steel shaft with a ball top, a plastic knob, and a coiled cable to one of the DE-9 control ports. Five moving electrical contacts and one mechanical centring mechanism, in a shell of black ABS.
roots.note: The C64's bundled joystick is a plain 2-button 4-way unit; the 3-button version came later and was supplied separately or with the C64C. Commodore also sold a version with a fire button on the shaft and a third button on the knob top ('Commodore 4611' and successors are cited for these in the retro literature, but I could not verify a Commodore part number for the specific 1982 bundle and have not asserted one).

facts.label: Centring
facts.value: 4 torsion/coil springs, not a positional detent

facts.label: Cable
facts.value: coiled, terminating in a DE-9 male plug

children.name: 4-way direction gate
children.description: A cross-shaped sliding gate that physically interlocks so only one of the four directions can be closed at a time - the same gating trick as a keyboard's 3-key rollover prevention. The gate rides on four ribs and is held centred by four springs, so it is self-centring and has no detented 'gate 2' half-way position.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: moulded glass-filled nylon or PBT gate on an ABS chassis

facts.label: Gating
facts.value: one direction at a time; diagonals blocked

facts.label: Return
facts.value: four coil or torsion springs on the gate ribs

children.name: Centring springs
children.description: Four small compression or torsion springs push the gate back to neutral from every direction. They are the part that wears out: once the springs weaken, the stick stays pushed, which is the most common repair on a vintage joystick and the reason 'joystick centering' appears in every retro repair guide.

facts.label: Service life
facts.value: the limiting part; springs lose tension and occasionally snap

children.name: Spring wire for the centring springs
children.description: Drawn music-wire or stainless spring wire, coiled and closed. Centring springs are the cheapest consumable in the whole joystick and the one that is always replaced rather than repaired.

children.name: Iron ore for the spring wire
children.description: The same ore-to-bar-to-wire chain as every other steel spring on the machine.

children.name: Why springs are the failure point
children.description: Gate springs carry the whole centring duty and are cycled by every direction press. Once one is weakened the stick sits off-centre and the machine reads a direction the user is not pressing - the most common single joystick fault of the era.

children.name: Bushing and friction washer
children.description: The shaft is supported by a plastic bushing or a nylon washer in the chassis, and a felt or fibre friction pad under the gate sets the feel. Friction pads compress and shed debris with age, which is the second classic cause of a stiff or drifting stick.
children.note: Friction pads are standard in this class of joystick; I have not measured the C64's.

children.name: Nylon bushing in the chassis
children.description: A moulded nylon bushing in the ABS chassis that the steel shaft runs in. Nylon is used because it is self-lubricating and will not gall the shaft; a metal bushing would seize onto the shaft as it rimes.

children.name: Nylon resin for the bushing
children.description: A lubricated or unfilled nylon grade, chosen for low friction against steel. Nylon-6-6 from caprolactam, the same polymer as the microswitch case.

children.name: Caprolactam
children.description: The caprolactam-to-nylon-6-6 chain. The joystick contains nylon in its bushing, its microswitch cases and its knob overmould.

children.name: Benzene from a steam cracker
children.description: Aromatic hydrocarbon recovered from the aromatics complex of a large cracker or from catalytic reforming of naphtha. The root of styrene, phenol, cumene, aniline and bisphenol.

children.name: Friction pad
children.description: A small felt or fibre pad under the gate that sets the lateral friction. Felt pads need almost no oil, dry-run cleanly, and shed a black dust that eventually gums the gate if the stick is never cleaned.

children.name: Wool felt
children.description: Pressed wool felt sets the lateral friction of the gate. Unlike an oiled pad it needs no lubricant, which matters because an oiled pad in a 1982 joystick attracts dust and eventually gums.

children.name: Four miniature microswitches
children.description: Four sealed miniature switches under the gate, one per direction. Each is a plastic case with a plunger and a fixed leaf plus a sprung leaf, gold-plated so the contact resistance stays low through millions of actuations. The plunger is depressed by a rib on the gate as it slides.

facts.label: Contacts
facts.value: gold-plated on brass or phosphor bronze

facts.label: Case
facts.value: moulded thermoset or thermoplastic body, sealed or dust-covered

children.name: Sprung leaf and contact-plating detail
children.description: Inside each switch a formed leaf is bowed against a fixed contact; pressing the plunger straightens the leaf onto it. The contacts are gold-plated over nickel because a joystick switch is a low-current, high-cycle signal contact where a stable millivolt-level resistance matters, and because the leaf is wiped clean on every actuation.
children.note: Gold-plated microswitch contacts are correct for the era; many cost-built equivalents were silver- or nickel-plated instead.

children.name: Gold plating of the microswitch leaf
children.description: The contact is gold-plated over nickel so its resistance stays at the millivolt level through millions of cycles. Gold leaf contacts in this class of switch were a real reliability advantage over the silver and nickel contacts used in cheaper equivalents.

children.name: Brass leaf metal
children.description: Phosphor bronze or brass strip, stamped and formed into a bowed leaf. Copper alloy from mined ore, as everywhere else in this file.

children.name: Switch case polymer
children.description: A small moulded case in a filled thermoset or a glass-filled nylon, chosen so the case survives being dropped off a desk with the stick still in hand - which, for a joystick sold with a computer, was a frequent event.

children.name: Glass-filled nylon case
children.description: A glass-filled nylon case gives a microswitch enough stiffness to keep its contact force with a thin wall, and enough toughness to survive being dropped. It is the standard material for that class of switch through the 1980s.

children.name: Nylon-6-6 resin
children.description: Caprolactam polymerisation - the same chain as the switch body and the keycap legend. A single C64 contains nylon in its switch housings, its joystick bushings and its microswitch cases.

children.name: Through-hole mounting and solder lugs
children.description: The switches are pushed into holes in the joystick's printed board and their pins soldered from underneath. Positioning them on that board is what sets how far the gate has to travel before a direction registers - the mechanical timing of the whole joystick.

children.name: Joystick switch board
children.description: A small printed board inside the joystick carries the four microswitches and drops the switch pins to the cable. It is a two-layer FR-4 board with the same glass-epoxy laminate and copper foil as the keyboard board.

children.name: Steel shaft and ball top
children.description: A cross-section steel shaft pressed into the gate, rising through the chassis with a moulded ball or ball-and-paddle top at the user end. The ball is the most-comforted part of the design and is also the part that wears smooth or cracks in old machines.

facts.label: Shaft
facts.value: ~6 mm square steel section, pressed into the gate

facts.label: Top
facts.value: moulded ball or ball-and-paddle, ~20 mm diameter

children.name: Cold-drawn steel bar
children.description: Mild or low-alloy steel, cold-drawn to a square section and cut to length. The gate's press fit is what locates the shaft; the steel is unplated except where it passes through the chassis, where corrosion is a genuine failure mode on a machine stored in a damp shed.

facts.label: Corrosion
facts.value: the shaft rimes in place in the bushing, freezing the stick

children.note: The frozen-shaft failure is well documented across the vintage joystick genre; the steel chain itself belongs to the metals file.

children.name: Iron ore (limonite / hematite)
children.description: The steel shaft begins as iron ore. The bulk of world steel in 1982 was made in a blast furnace from sintered hematite-magnetite pellets/coke, refined to steel in a basic oxygen furnace. Rust and pitting on a forty-year-old joystick shaft is this ore still trying to get out.
children.note: The blast-furnace coke chain belongs to the power file; referenced here.

facts.label: Route
facts.value: blast furnace -> basic oxygen furnace -> continuous cast bar

children.name: Pelletising and blast furnace
children.description: Concentrate is pelletised and fired with limestone and coke, charged with the coke burden, and reduced to pig iron. The coke is what makes it economically possible, and it is where the energy density that lets a steel part cost less than a plastic one comes from.

children.name: Metallurgical coke
children.description: Coking coal heated in coke ovens to drive off the volatile matter, leaving a porous carbon fuel that is also the reducing agent. Mined coal, and the reason a 1982 steel plant sits next to a coking battery.

children.name: ABS knob and top button
children.description: The moulded handle on the top of the shaft. On a 2-button unit it is a plain grip knob; on a 3-button unit a fire switch is moulded into the shaft and a third button into the knob's top, sprung against the shaft and actuated by a rod inside it. Black ABS, textured on the grip faces.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: ABS, sometimes with a soft TPE or rubber overmould

children.note: A soft overmould on the grip was a quality feature on some 1980s sticks and absent on the cheap bundled ones; I cannot say which the C64 bundle shipped with.

children.name: ABS (acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene)
children.description: The workhorse thermoplastic of consumer electronics housings in 1982: injection mouldable to a hard gloss surface, tough enough for a hand-held knob, and cheap. The same material as the keycaps, and largely the same hydrocarbon feedstock.

facts.label: Melt flow
facts.value: chosen grade ~5-15 g/10 min for housings

children.note: The styrene and butadiene chains are expanded at c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs; referenced rather than duplicated.

children.name: Glass or mineral filler and the TiO2 whitener
children.description: The knob's black colour is a pigment - usually a carbon black or an iron oxide - dispersed in the ABS. Where a lighter colour was wanted the pigment was titanium dioxide, a white pigment made from ilmenite, and it is the same titanium chain as the barium titanate capacitor powder.
children.note: The titanium dioxide route is shared with the MLCC powder tree at mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.synthesis.titanium-dioxide; referenced rather than duplicated.

children.name: Pigment dispersion in the ABS
children.description: The colourant is dispersed into the polymer in a compounding extruder before the moulding, not added at the press. A black joystick knob therefore contains a few per cent of carbon black and an antioxidant package.

children.name: Titanium dioxide whitener
children.description: Where a lighter colour was used, the whitener was rutile TiO2 from ilmenite - the same titanium chain as the barium titanate powder.

children.name: Alumina from bauxite
children.description: Smelter-grade alumina, 99.5-99.7 % Al2O3, from the Bayer process. The substrate material for ceramic discs and MLCCs, the can material for resistors, and the dielectric feedstock for the barium titanate chain.

children.name: Bauxite profile
children.description: A soft, deeply weathered tropical profile of hydrated aluminium oxides; mined in open pits, often a few tens of metres thick, sitting directly on the aluminous bedrock.

children.name: Injection moulding of the knob
children.description: The knob is a two-shot or single-shot ABS moulding, often with a moulded-in texture or a soft overmould. It has to be comfortable and it has to stay on the shaft for decades.

children.name: Knob mould tool
children.description: A hardened steel cavity tool, polished so the knob has a gloss finish. Thousands of knobs per tool life; the polish is the difference between a shiny knob and a matt one.

children.name: Iron ore
children.description: Hematite and magnetite, the iron ore of the world trade. Everything ferrous in this file - springs, shafts, stamping dies, tool steel, cast-iron kiln parts - begins here.

children.name: Fire button on shaft and knob
children.description: On 3-button sticks a fire switch is moulded into the shaft itself and a third button into the knob top, actuated by a rod inside the shaft. Each is a miniature microswitch of the same family as the direction switches.

children.name: Coiled cable and DE-9 plug
children.description: A coiled cable of seven or nine conductors leaving the chassis bottom, terminating in a DE-9 male plug that looks mechanically identical to the socket it plugs into but has male pins. The plug's contacts are gold-flashed brass, made the same way and by the same stamping and plating route as the socket contacts on the machine.
children.note: The coiled cable was traditionally PVC-insulated stranded copper; some units shipped with a straight lead. The number of conductors varies between joystick models and I have not verified the C64 bundle's exactly.

children.name: DE-9 male plug contacts
children.description: Stamped brass pins, gold-flashed over nickel, moulded into a thermoplastic D-shell that keys to the socket's D-shape. Because the D-shell is polarised, the plug physically cannot be inserted backwards - the same mechanical trick as the moulded keyway on a D-sub generally.
children.note: The stamping, forming and plating route is described at c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.

children.name: Cable assembly and strain relief
children.description: The conductors are crimped into the DE-9 pins and the cable is clamped by a moulded strain relief at the shell, so bending the cable does not work the pin out of the crimp. Strain relief is the single cheapest thing that decides whether a peripheral cable survives five years of use.

children.name: Stranded conductor
children.description: Fine-stranded copper, tinned, for flexibility. Seven or nine of them, depending on the joystick model - the C64 reads five signals plus the common and the fire button.

children.name: Tinning of the conductor
children.description: The stranded conductor is tinned so the crimp barrel grips cleanly and the joint is solderable. Tin from cassiterite, in a peripheral cable a few centimetres from the machine.
